We introduce algebraic objects, analogous to matroids, which enable the study of elements of $GL_n(\mathbb{F})$ through an exterior algebra-like matroid structure. This work generalizes classical matroid ranks and extends various properties of matroids, applicable to any commutative ring $\mathbb{F}$.

In the context of spoken dialogue systems, effectively handling ambiguity in spoken input is a critical aspect. The uncertainty in speech recognition can be quantified by the similarity between the most likely and second likely word sequences, and this concept is extended to the identification of the top-performing audio recordings for specific words. We introduce a method for training confusion networks that captures the likelihood of alternative word pronunciations, and demonstrate its utility in downstream tasks such as dialogue state tracking. The approach involves using a phoneme-level network to predict the probability of alternative pronunciations, and this prediction is then used to prevent the system from inferring incorrect user intentions based on misidentified words. The proposed method has shown significant improvements in intent recognition accuracy, achieving gains of up to 10% on a challenging dataset.

We establish a formula for the number of Grothendieck sheaves of specific rank and degree on a smooth projective curve within a fixed genus, which have a specified Jordan-H\"older filtration, calculated by modulating the rank and degree. This outcome is achieved through an inductive reasoning process that leverages the geometric properties of the curve's Brill-Noether variety, thereby providing an alternative method for determining its dimension.

A critical component in distributed systems is often represented as a collection of substructures, such as matrices, where a request to the system can only be fulfilled if all constituent parts are available. In an effort to optimize storage, researchers have developed an approach known as universal access structures, which minimize the size of these collection structures, thereby reducing the overall storage requirements. The efficiency of this approach is measured by comparing the maximum collection size to the minimum collection size defined by the input structure's submatrix count. Recent studies have shown that there are cases where the optimal universal access structure results in collection sizes that are exponentially larger than the minimum collection size, rendering these universal access structures impractical for optimized distributed storage.

We introduce a method for accurately estimating entanglement in mixed states of optical qubits by utilizing a tailored measurement approach. Our optimal strategy enables precise characterization of qudit systems up to a certain level of complexity. Our results indicate that specific multi-particle methods outperform others in estimating entanglement, and we demonstrate this by providing a successful estimation protocol for optimal quantum computing strategies involving multiple photons.

The long-lived, electron-depleted core of the H-mode plasmas in the JET tokamak has been found to be associated with large-scale, coherent structures known as "palm tree modes" (PTMs). These structures have been observed to form gradually over a 10-20 second period, and their appearance is often accompanied by a noticeable increase in the edge recycling rate. A closer examination of the PTMs using high-resolution edge plasma measurements has allowed researchers to pinpoint their origin to the core region, rather than the edge. Furthermore, analysis of the PTMs' spatial patterns and power spectra has revealed that they are consistent with a type of mode called "ballooning modes." A theoretical model has been developed to explain the growth of these PTMs, and it is found that their appearance is a natural consequence of the evolution of the core region's characteristics. The model also suggests that the periodic disappearance of the core region is linked to the growth of the PTMs.

A basic approach utilizing word embeddings and a non-linear classifier is presented as a benchmark for both continual learning and random initialization of classifiers. The benchmark's performance, evaluated using standard metrics such as final accuracy, forgetting, and the Jensen-Shannon divergence, demonstrates that a linear classifier with word embeddings can achieve competitive results on the standard benchmark datasets. The research also reveals that fine-tuning these embeddings leads to improved performance, a finding that is contrary to the expectations of the research community. The outcome suggests that CTL methods relying on pre-trained models may not always be necessary, and that a linear classifier can perform surprisingly well, even outdoing more complex models in some cases.

This study introduces an innovative framework for identifying hate speech across multiple media types, including text and images. Building on the success of deep learning models, our approach integrates pre-trained text and image representations to create a comprehensive multimodal system. A key component of this framework is the incorporation of a multimodal attention mechanism, which enables precise identification of the most significant features from each media type. This results in enhanced detection capabilities and an understanding of the importance of different modalities in the context of hate speech. Furthermore, our model is validated using a large dataset of Instagram captions and their corresponding images, which is made available for public use.

We investigate the behavior of large networks of theta neurons, where a specific type of nonlinear interaction is considered, under stochastic influence. The probabilistic connection between neurons is modeled using random network structures, with analysis focusing on the effects of varying network topologies on collective behavior. By employing mean-field theory, it is shown that the distribution of neuronal connections significantly impacts the collective phase transitions, particularly the degree distribution of highly connected neurons. Furthermore, it is found that the stochastic nature of neuronal connections can alter the collective phase transitions, even when the average connectivity remains constant, leading to the emergence of new types of collective behavior.

Recent advancements in Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have led to significant success in Automatic Program Repair (APR) by utilizing patches that transform buggy code into correct versions. Current APR models often rely on the assumption that a single buggy version of a program corresponds to a single buggy location, which is often inaccurate. To address this limitation, a novel approach called Adversarial Patch Generation (APG) has been developed, which generates a set of possible buggy locations for each buggy program version and then uses a subsequent DNN to identify the most likely buggy location. Our experiments, conducted on a large dataset of Java programs, demonstrate that APG outperforms state-of-the-art APR methods by a substantial margin, with improvements of up to 10% in accuracy.

This research paper examines the capacity region of a generalized interference channel with a finite number of antennas at each node, under constraints of limited power and finite alphabet size for messages and messages, as well as unlimited transmission time. We introduce a two-way interference channel as an equivalent model to the GIFC and derive a capacity region for it by establishing a cut-set upper bound and a rate limit lower bound. By applying a time-sharing argument, we narrow the gap between the two bounds to a specific range. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the obtained capacity region is indeed applicable to the GIFC by establishing a maximum achievable rate and showing that it closely approximates the true capacity region, ultimately proving that the gap between the obtained capacity region and the actual capacity region is bounded.

In the study of heavy-ion collisions, the flow of particles produced at high energies is analyzed to understand the properties of the quark-gluon plasma. This study focuses on the connection between flow analysis techniques used in experiments and simulations. By comparing the eccentricity of the initial state to the observed symmetry of the final state, researchers can gain insights into the equation-of-state of the plasma. This technique, known as the $\varPsi_2$-$\varepsilon_2$ relation, is explored in detail and its implications for understanding the properties of the plasma are discussed.

The rapid spread of COVID-19 has been a major concern, with the disease infecting a vast number of people and causing numerous fatalities. The detection of COVID-19 through chest X-ray imaging has gained attention due to its speed and efficiency. Deep learning models have been utilized to analyze COVID-19 patients' chest CT scans, showcasing promising results. However, concerns regarding the security of these models have been raised, with the potential for malicious actors to manipulate the data and compromise the accuracy of the models. To address these issues, this research proposes an innovative approach that combines privacy preservation and security measures. By employing adversarial training, our method aims to develop a robust COVID-19 detection model that can withstand attacks and safeguard sensitive patient data. Our findings demonstrate that this approach effectively balances accuracy and security, paving the way for the development of more secure and reliable AI-powered medical systems.

This study presents a decentralized inference framework using graph neural networks (GNNs) for wireless communication systems. The framework integrates wireless networking and deep learning via the message passing algorithm, allowing GNNs to be trained and executed across a distributed network of wireless nodes. Each node processes and exchanges information based on its local data and that of its neighboring nodes, ultimately enabling the network to make accurate predictions. To facilitate efficient gNN implementation, the framework incorporates a compiler that translates standard GNN code into optimized code tailored to heterogeneous wireless node architectures. The results demonstrate the framework's ability to achieve high accuracy in wireless communication tasks, such as channel estimation, while also offering improved computational efficiency and performance scalability.

Göias, the 5th most populous state in Brazil, has been plagued by high levels of homicide, accounting for 10% of the country's total deaths from 2002 to 2014. An examination of annual data from 2002 to 2014 for all of Göias, along with its municipalities, has been conducted to identify patterns of violence. Göias, divided into four distinct regions, has shown significant disparities in homicide rates, with the western and northern areas experiencing lower levels of violence compared to the eastern and central regions.

We've developed an innovative stochastic gradient descent method that dynamically adjusts its step size based on the level of data variance and problem landscape, and a corresponding variant for addressing catastrophic gradient acceleration. This method's theoretical framework is grounded in a novel Lyapunov function that captures the problem's curvature, and its efficacy is demonstrated through its performance on both standard and enhanced gradient scenarios. Furthermore, this algorithm has been successfully applied to a range of problems, including those with concave-convex-convex loss functions and high-dimensional data, and its implementation has been shown to be efficient and scalable.

The sun's core is shrouded in mystery, and to date, no direct observations have been made. The theory of nuclear fusion, first proposed by Bethe in 1939, has been proven through indirect means, but its inner workings remain unknown. The key lies in detecting gamma-ray bursts resulting from fusion, but the high energy of these photons makes direct detection impossible. To overcome this, researchers are developing solar hard X-ray observatories, such as BabyIAXO, to study solar neutrino-like phenomena. The mini-Astronomical X-ray Spectro-polarimetry Imager for the Sun will capture X-ray images of the sun's interior, providing new insights into the fusion process. The device will be able to distinguish between X-rays produced by different fusion reactions, providing a detailed understanding of the sun's inner workings.

The occupation number of quasiparticles in a superconductor's gap can remain stable or fluctuate autonomously, depending on the dynamics. When fluctuations occur, specific conditions must be satisfied, notably in relation to the phase of the quasiparticle self-energy, a parameter influenced by the electron-electron interaction. Notably, this relative phase can be dynamically adjusted by an applied microwave field, opening up the possibility for developing autonomous gap modulators operating in the mixed state of superconductors.

Developing a reliable and versatile robotic grasp control system is a critical component in creating an efficient and adaptable system. To achieve this, researchers have been employing deep learning-based grasp control networks, which rely on extensive training data to reach their full potential. To facilitate this, researchers have been utilizing dexterous hands with advanced force control capabilities, allowing for more natural and dexterous grasping techniques. In this study, we introduce DexGraspNet, a large-scale dataset comprising over 1.2 million dexterous grasp samples, surpassing the current record of 250,000 samples. We also introduce a novel simulation environment that accurately models dexterous grasping tasks and demonstrates the effectiveness of our dataset in training a dexterous grasp control network.

A novel MRI technique is introduced that capitalizes on the inherent motion compensation capabilities of a multidimensional turbo spin-echo sequence. This approach is particularly effective in a field of view of 400x400 mm, and it is implemented in a 3 Tesla scanner. The technique was applied to a study involving 15 healthy volunteers and 12 patients, and it was compared to conventional MRI images. Additionally, a simulation was conducted to evaluate the technique's performance in the presence of respiratory motion, and it was found that the novel method significantly outperformed traditional motion correction techniques. Overall, the novel approach resulted in high-resolution images with superior quality, and it was successfully applied to produce high-quality four-dimensional T2-weighted turbo spin-echo sequences.

A new approach called InDistill has been developed to leverage smaller, less complex models by transferring the essential details of larger, more effective models. This is achieved through a distillation process that preserves the flow of information between layers. InDistill utilizes layers with the same architecture, applying both teacher and student layers across multiple networks to capture teacher internal knowledge. Experimental results on image classification and super-resolution tasks demonstrate that InDistill yields superior performance compared to existing model compression methods.

Two submersion functions from the set of two-dimensional real numbers to the set of real numbers are considered, and it's shown that topological equivalence of the functions is a consequence of the same for their respective linear-like foliations.

Ecosystems with mobile herbivory can significantly influence plant growth and the environment. To better understand this, a mathematical model is proposed that takes into account the movement of grazers and the resulting resource distribution. By using a mathematical approach, it's found that a system with herbivory and the associated non-local grazing effect is stable and effective in maintaining the ecosystem's balance. This outcome suggests that the movement of grazers can have a stabilizing effect on the ecosystem, and that the unique characteristics of the system, such as the Gaussian distribution of herbivory, contribute to this effect.

The widely used sketching algorithm CountSketch effectively reduces matrix multiplication into simpler dot product calculations. This matrix multiplication can be thought of as a game where a matrix A and a vector x engage in a round-based competition. In each turn, x selects a coordinate to reveal a single entry of A, and CountSketch can only track a limited number of these selected entries. CountSketch's ability to reconstruct A's product with x depends on how x chooses these selected entries. Previous research has shown CountSketch can be weak when x's choices are random and strong when x's choices are carefully planned. This paper introduces a new class of vectors that allows CountSketch to be effective even with some x's choices being random. Our results show CountSketch can be robust against adaptive inputs by carefully selecting a small number of entries in each turn. This choice can be made without knowing future x's moves. Our findings also reveal that making such an optimal choice may require a significant number of CountSketch's resources when x's choices are planned. This choice can be made without knowing future x's moves.

The ipie package is a Python-based auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo software designed to solve the electronic Schrödinger equation using a stochastic approach. This package, with its emphasis on flexibility and performance, supports parallel processing on both CPU and GPU architectures. It features a comprehensive set of quantum chemistry tools for generating zero-order wave functions and auxiliary-operator expansions, as well as an array of customizability options for users to tailor the zero-order wave function generator, auxiliary-operator expansion, and auxiliary-field stochastic process to optimize computational efficiency. This package's implementation of GPU acceleration via the PyTorch library enables significant speed improvements, making ipie an efficient and versatile tool for electronic structure calculations.

The classic Prisoner's Dilemma game has been reimagined as a strategic opportunity for high-frequency trading in the quantum era. By harnessing quantum strategies, traders can potentially outmaneuver competitors and exploit non-local correlations. A comprehensive trade model has been formulated to analyze various quantum and classical approaches, including a comparison of quantum strategies in a no-reward scenario versus a one-reward scenario. Notably, the former revealed a trader's advantage in the quantum domain, whereas the latter showcased an adversary's advantage. Furthermore, experimental results from the IBM quantum computer have demonstrated the feasibility of this trade model, paving the way for further quantum-inspired trading innovations.

A key challenge for service providers is optimizing their pricing strategies when intermediaries are involved. Specifically, cloud service providers aim to set prices for resources to maximize revenue from enterprises, but often rely on IT managers to complete the order process. The behavior of these managers is influenced by a utility function that considers their personal gain and effort costs. The personal benefit they receive is determined by a combination of their enjoyment of the product and the financial reward from a percentage of the service provider's invoice. The service provider's goal is to maximize revenue by adjusting the price of resources, while the IT managers choose which enterprises to serve based on maximizing their personal gain. The equilibrium outcome of this interaction is a combination of the service provider's optimal pricing strategy and the managers' selection of enterprises to serve. The service provider can use this information to determine the best pricing strategy that maximizes revenue. The model is applied to two scenarios: one where managers can choose from multiple enterprises and another where they can only choose one. The model shows that the service provider can benefit from the presence of a self-interested intermediary, as the optimal strategy in this case yields higher revenue than the ideal scenario where the intermediary is cooperative. The service provider can also use the model to determine the optimal level of commission to set for the intermediary, which can result in higher revenue than the ideal scenario.

To facilitate abstractive summarization, we've developed an entity-aware model 
capable of generating existing names rather than creating new entities. This model 
utilizes a pre-trained language model, which we've adapted through a planning 
framework that enables step-by-step generation with entity-based decision making. 
In contrast to traditional encoder-decoder models, this approach outperforms them in
planning with entity-prompts, which serve as a bridge between tokens to improve 
summarization coherence.

This research presents new sufficient conditions for differentiating a function with n real variables, where these conditions are grounded in the differentiability of a related function with n-1 variables and are less restrictive than traditional criteria.

Human vocal synchrony in social interactions is a natural phenomenon that reflects our deep connection with others. By analyzing conversations between pairs of people, we developed an automated method to measure synchronized speech patterns. Our approach, which measures vocal synchrony, demonstrates higher accuracy compared to traditional methods that rely on fixed windows. By comparing our approach with established methods, we found it achieves a significant performance boost of 15% in various real-world speech datasets. Furthermore, we validated the importance of selecting optimal window sizes for accurate vocal synchrony detection.

A quantum control system's behavior is essentially the trajectory it takes on the unitary sphere, which can be represented as a specific kind of infinity-topological space known as a lambda-s1. This study explores the relationship between this space and a category of quantum control systems and their combined outputs, which is fully and accurately mirrored in the category of infinity-topological spaces and their combined outputs, thus showing that these categories are equivalent to each other.

Analytical calculations have been performed for the energy of two quasiparticle excitations within fractional quantum Hall states, yielding insights into their behavior. These computations, based on precise two-quasiparticle wavefunctions, show that, at sufficiently low temperatures, the energy of paired excitations is lower than that of individual excitations, a phenomenon that can be experimentally verified. Furthermore, the model predicts a relationship between the oscillation frequency of the two quasiparticle state and its angular momentum, a relationship that may be observable in experiments.

To tackle the computational challenges of solving glaciological models, a linear Stokes equations-based method is employed to simulate creep in flowing ice. This approach is particularly suited to flow over complex boundaries, where traditional techniques may be impractical. A second-order accurate and stable analysis of this method is provided, supported by finite element theory. This method is validated through a numerical experiment involving the simulation of a block of ice sliding down a plane.

We present the results of a deep VLT/OVS observation of the galaxy NGC 4485, a starbursting spiral galaxy, using the Optical Violent Tappert Element Telescope. The dataset includes VLT images across the galaxy's disk, covering its star-forming regions, as well as OVS data across the entire galaxy, including its hot halo. The VLT images show that the galaxy's disk has a uniform color, but its star-forming regions exhibit distinct patterns. The galaxy's starburst core is characterized by high gas content, a low metallicity, and a high star formation rate. The galaxy's hot halo exhibits a high temperature and a high velocity dispersion, indicating that it is being heated by the galaxy's starburst activity. The data also show that the galaxy's hot halo is being enriched by the galaxy's starburst activity, with the galaxy's disk serving as a reservoir of the enriched material. The findings support the hypothesis that galactic winds play a crucial role in regulating the formation of stars in starbursting galaxies.

Our research examines the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 30 and 40 GeV/GeV/c energy levels in various Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. We analyzed the evolution of anisotropic flow within the model, and found that higher energy collisions exhibit a notable increase in $v_3$ values, particularly at 40 GeV/GeV/c, which contrasts with the behavior of $v_2$. This phenomenon is attributed to the delayed phase transition in the higher energy collisions, which allows for a more pronounced development of $v_3$ values, whereas $v_2$ values decrease due to a more rapid development of anisotropic pressure.

This research introduces the Synchronous Robotic Framework (SRF), a unified platform that streamlines the development of complex autonomous systems. The SRF integrates key components, including a robot description file, world model, and control logic, to enable the efficient creation of autonomous systems. The platform is demonstrated through the implementation of a multi-robot system capable of performing coordinated tasks in a shared environment.

Deep neural networks for semantic segmentation have shown impressive results, but they have been largely dependent on large, labor-intensive datasets. A novel approach using self-supervised, monocular depth estimation is proposed as a means to improve pre-training for better segmentation results. Building on a successful combination of depth estimation and self-supervised segmentation from the SOLO-DLE method, our research explores the effectiveness of depth estimation in conjunction with self-supervised methods, specifically contrastive learning, in achieving better performance on down-stream segmentation tasks. Surprisingly, our experiments reveal that the depth estimation and contrastive learning combination does not yield improved results, and that the depth estimation component contributes minimally to the final outcome. These findings suggest that monocular depth estimation may not be a suitable feature for self-supervised semantic segmentation, and that the depth estimation and contrastive learning combination is not an effective approach for leveraging monocular depth estimation in a self-supervised setting.

This research establishes two primary objectives. Firstly, we derive the optimal Bohr radius for a specific type of log-harmonic mapping, denoted as $f$ with analytic part $h$ and anti-analytic part $\overline{g}$, where $h$ and $g$ belong to the class of univalent functions and are defined within the complex unit disk. The findings indicate that for such mappings, the sum of the absolute values of the coefficients of the Taylor series expansion does not exceed one, provided the complex variable's modulus is less than a specific optimal radius, determined by the minimum of two specific values derived from the mapping's coefficients. Secondly, we refine previous results by enhancing the Bohr radius for the class of log-harmonic mappings with star-like properties in a more general sense, thereby extending and improving existing knowledge in the field.

A novel nonparametric method has been developed for inferring Kendall's tau, a measure of dependence, by creating an asymptotically optimal score function through projection of the ideal metric. This score function leads to a faster and more stable estimator in comparison to traditional methods like Kendall's tau and Skorokhod's V-statistic. Simulations demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, which converges more rapidly to the limiting distribution, enabling efficient inference. Building on this work, a data-driven bandwidth selection method has been proposed for kernel smoothing estimators of Kendall's tau's influence function, utilizing knowledge of the Hessian matrix.

The integration of vehicles and artificial intelligence has led to the emergence of vehicle intelligence, a concept that encompasses a range of applications, from autonomous driving to infrastructure monitoring. As vehicle-mounted sensors generate vast amounts of data, edge computing has become a natural choice for processing this data, enabling faster response times and reduced transmission burdens. In vehicle edge intelligence, multiple AI models are trained collaboratively at the edge, while vehicle privacy must be maintained during this process. This paper proposes a comprehensive framework for privacy-preserving vehicle edge intelligence, incorporating federated learning, blockchain, and blockchain-based resource allocation. The framework addresses privacy concerns through the use of differential privacy, secure aggregation, and blockchain-based data verification, while leveraging blockchain's capabilities for resource management and AI model optimization. The results demonstrate the framework's effectiveness in enhancing vehicle edge intelligence while safeguarding sensitive data.

We introduce a novel class of surface representations, Euler Characteristic Surfaces, and demonstrate their capacity to accurately model intricate 3D shapes, including those with complex connectivity. By leveraging topological priors, our method achieves a notable reduction in model complexity, resulting in high-data efficiency. The success of Euler Characteristic Surfaces is attributed to their utilization of piecewise constant coordinate mappings, enabling the explicit representation of surface geometry. The rigidity of triangular meshes is preserved through an innovative encoding of surface normal fields, which we prove yields superior results compared to traditional normal-based representations. The efficacy of our approach is substantiated by extensive experiments on real-world datasets, where we observe substantial improvements in data efficiency and model performance.

This study examines the dynamics of a Holling-Tanner predator-prey model with the strong Allee effect affecting the prey population, and we derive conditions for local stability and perform a thorough linear stability analysis. Our analysis reveals the occurrence of Hopf bifurcations in the Holling-Tanner model with strong Allee effect under specific parameter conditions, and we conduct an in-depth bifurcation analysis to understand these phenomena. Additionally, in the context of zero net growth for prey populations at low densities, we investigate a degenerate Hopf bifurcation in the Holling-Tanner model with Michaelis-Menten response. Furthermore, we analyze the global dynamics of this model and confirm the persistence of both species, as well as demonstrate the emergence of stable, periodic solutions in the system.

This study builds on a series of earlier works by the author, specifically references 1, 2, and 3, to further develop an asymptotic analysis of a specific variant of the ellipsoidal facet pivot method for solving linear programming problems. Prior works, including references 1 and 2, laid the groundwork for this development. Under the assumption that the initial starting point is arbitrarily far from the optimal solution, a specific variant of the ellipsoidal facet pivot method was proposed, which is guaranteed to converge to the optimal solution within a specific number of iterations. Furthermore, under the additional assumption that the optimal solution lies within a specific geometric shape, a more precise upper bound on the number of iterations was derived.

We explore the skew polynomial ring $R[x;\sigma,\alpha]$ derived from an abelian finite mixed torsion group $\varphi$ with a basis that generates a sequence $[\alpha_0, \alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n]$, and establish an isomorphism between the first NK1 functor of the monoid of units in $U_n(R[\varphi];\Delta)$ and the quotient $\varphi_1/\varphi_n$.

This paper examines how the inclusion of off-shell effects influences the top quark mass derived from $t\bar{t}$j events, and reveals that these effects are substantial, amounting to approximately 0.7 GeV. A method for consistently taking off-shell contributions into account is proposed, and the resulting top quark mass correction is found to be around 0.7 GeV, comparable to the scale and size of the NLO QCD correction.

The growing threat of deceptive anti-spoofing attacks poses a significant challenge to the performance of facial recognition systems, which are widely used in security applications. To counter this, researchers have developed anti-spoofing modules that can identify deceptive images and improve the performance of recognition systems. However, the effectiveness of these modules can be compromised when they are trained and tested on different domains, which is a common scenario in real-world applications. To address this issue, a novel zero-shot approach is proposed, which involves training a vision transformer-based network to detect deceptive features in images without any labeled data. The proposed method outperforms the state-of-the-art anti-spoofing modules on several benchmark datasets, including CASIA-A, WSPU, and LFW-AI, and also exhibits robustness against various data augmentation techniques.

Deep reinforcement learning has emerged as a promising technique for autonomous driving, offering a range of applications including vehicle control, decision-making, and mapping. This paper outlines the capabilities of deep reinforcement learning in autonomous driving and presents a comprehensive framework that covers the entire driving process. The framework is divided into three key components: perception, decision-making, and planning. Each component is analyzed with a focus on the strengths and limitations of deep reinforcement learning, as well as the challenges associated with its application. The paper also discusses the integration of multiple tasks and the potential for combining different methods to achieve a fully automated driving system.

Evolutionary algorithms can be efficiently parallelized on high-performance computing systems using asynchronous evaluation, which eliminates unnecessary waiting times. However, this parallelization method introduces an unwanted side effect where individuals with lower fitness are evaluated more slowly, leading to a higher chance of being eliminated before they have a fair opportunity to reproduce. To address this issue, a new parent selection strategy has been developed that takes into account the evaluation frequencies of all individuals, including both their fitness and sampling rates, to minimize the adverse impact of asynchronous evaluation on the algorithm's overall performance. Experimental results have demonstrated the effectiveness of this strategy in reducing evaluation time bias and improving the overall performance of multi-objective evolutionary algorithms.

The recent analysis of the OGLE-2017-BLG-1434 microlensing event revealed the presence of a 3.7 M_J planet orbiting a 0.4 M_sun star. This finding was based on the analysis of the light curve, which showed a deviation caused by the gravitational interaction between the two objects. The data indicated that the angular separation between the objects was approximately 1.2 arcseconds. A follow-up study, which involved the use of Keck/NIRC2 infrared imaging, further constrained the size of the host star to be within 1.2-1.6 kpc. The analysis showed that the OGLE-2017-BLG-1434 system could be either a cold planet orbiting a low-mass star or a warm planet orbiting a high-mass star. The study also found that the OGLE-2017-BLG-1434 system is likely to be an exoplanetary system with a high mass ratio and a high eccentricity.

The high-frequency expansion of the time-periodic Lindbladians was derived and analyzed to determine its relationship to the Lindblad generators of transformed time-averaged Lindblad equations. By introducing novel similarity transformations, we can in certain cases simplify the analysis and calculate the effective time-periodic Lindblad generators. These can then be used to model phenomena such as driving-driven quantum systems, where the principles of high-frequency expansions are applied to compute dynamics. To illustrate the high-frequency expansion's utility, we derived an explicit expression for the time-evolution of the quantum dynamics.

We have conducted an in-depth study of the local magnetic structure in CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ ($x$ = 0.15, 0.2, 0.25) using neutron reflectometry. The research revealed that spin fluctuations in these materials are strongly influenced by the presence of Rh. The addition of Rh causes the materials to deviate from long-range magnetic order and enter a state of freezing, with the rate of freezing varying depending on the Rh concentration. The materials exhibit a temperature-dependent change in their magnetic properties, with the rate of change decreasing as the Rh concentration increases. The materials' magnetic properties are also affected by the presence of structural defects and impurities.

A newly identified large-scale HI self-absorption feature has been discovered in the vicinity of G176.51+00.20, a high-mass star-forming region. This distinctive feature is thought to be a result of a cold, dense foreground structure absorbing HI emission from the background. The formation of such structures is thought to be linked to star formation, particularly in the vicinity of high-mass star-forming regions. Our research reveals that these structures are located within the vicinity of G176.51+00.20, with temperatures of approximately 50 Kelvin and a mass density of approximately 1.0 particles per cubic centimeter. A comparative analysis of such structures in the vicinity of G176.51+00.20 and other high-mass star-forming regions indicates that they are relatively young and may be a crucial component in the process of star formation.

We demonstrate the topological equivalence of all intermediate beta-transformations to certain greedy beta-transformations that incorporate a hole, thereby linking this equivalence to the study of return times in these beta-transformations.

Determining the CP-violating phase phi_s in Bs decays into specific final states that include both J/psi and pi particles has been attempted using data collected at the LHCb experiment during 2011. The phi_s phase was measured in the Bs decays into both J/psi pi+ pi- final states, with an average value of -0.04 degrees and an associated uncertainty of 5 degrees. The phi_s phase is an essential parameter in the CKM matrix that can provide evidence for the predicted but yet unobserved b-s transitions involving virtual particles.

In this research, we determine the minimum number of arcs within the plane $\mathbb F_q^2$ that satisfy specific conditions. Specifically, an arc has a property where every pair of points is connected by a unique line that doesn't include a third point from the arc. By establishing a construction method, we show that any arc larger than a certain size, roughly $\sqrt{q}$ points, must be an arc in the traditional sense. Furthermore, through analysis involving sums over characters, we prove that the minimum number of arcs in $\mathbb F_q^2$ grows at a rate of $q^3$ as $q$ increases.

A pictorial proof shows that there are $\binom{n+2}{4}$ equilateral triangles in a regular $n$-sided triangle by establishing a one-to-one correspondence between four-element subsets of the set $\{1,2,...,n+2\}$ and the equilateral triangles in this grid, where it is visually represented without the use of words.

Recent advances in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated their potential in addressing complex real-world challenges. However, GNNs' reliance on multiple message-passing stages can lead to network overfitting and hinder interpretability. To address this issue, we propose the Parameterized Explainer (PE), a novel method that enhances the understanding of GNN predictions by analyzing the influence of individual nodes on its outcomes. Unlike previous approaches, PE incorporates a parameterized graph attention mechanism to capture node interactions more effectively, allowing for more precise identification of influential nodes. Our experiments on real-world datasets show PE's superior performance in exploring node interactions and providing more accurate explanations.

The peculiar cluster, RXCJ0232.2-4420, contains a significant amount of substructure, which is evident in X-ray and radio emissions. This makes it an ideal subject for a comprehensive study of its substructure. Using a combination of XMM-Newton and Chandra X-ray data, we have analyzed the structure of the X-ray emitting gas in the cluster. Our analysis reveals that the gas has a relatively low temperature of 10.2 keV and a relatively low metal abundance of 0.27. Additionally, we have identified two substructures within the cluster, which are located in the southern and northern regions. These substructures are characterized by lower temperatures and lower entropy, and they are likely to be the remnants of infalling galaxies. Our study also shows that the X-ray emission in the southern region is consistent with the thermal emission from the gas, which is heated by the shock waves produced by the moving galaxy.

Recently, the Legendre Memory Unit (LMU) has emerged as a groundbreaking family of recurrent neural networks, offering superior performance in long-term dependency tasks while being more computationally efficient and biologically plausible than its primary competitor, the LSTM. Despite LMU's advantages, training large models using this architecture poses a significant challenge due to its non-differentiable memory access mechanism, which necessitates the use of the path integral rule and results in lengthy computation times. To address this issue, we present a straightforward method for vectorizing the backward pass, thereby facilitating efficient GPU computation. Our approach yields a 100x speedup over the original implementation, enabling the training of large-scale LMU models with an average batch size of 1024 over 100 epochs.

A newly emerging field in particle physics is centered around the possibility of the existence of very weakly interacting particles. The exploration of such particles is crucial as it could potentially explain fundamental cosmic phenomena, such as dark matter and neutrino properties, as well as test theories beyond the Standard Model. The following review will cover recent advancements in experimental searches for such particles, focusing on experiments conducted between 2017 and 2018.

Language development is a complex process that involves the migration of people and the exchange of ideas.  In this study, we investigate how a particular aspect of language, known as coherence, naturally arises during language evolution.  We have created a model that simulates this process using the naming game and found evidence of coherent language development even without people consciously working towards it.  The results show that language development can be understood as a natural phenomenon that occurs during migration and cultural exchange.

We examine a system of two waves that interact over a fixed domain in n-dimensional space, where one wave experiences Kelvin-Voigt damping that is applied only within a limited area. The system's long-term behavior under such conditions is investigated, revealing that it achieves global stability with an exponential rate if the region of applied damping intersects with the area where the two waves intersect harmonically, and it achieves a polynomial stability rate if this condition is not met.

In recent years, deep reinforcement learning has demonstrated remarkable success in solving complex tasks. Nevertheless, the rapid advancement in this field has led to the creation of powerful agents that often lack transparency in their decision-making processes. To address this limitation, this research introduces a novel, model-based hierarchical reinforcement learning approach, incorporating inductive logic programming to provide an interpretable framework for understanding agent behavior. By decomposing the learning process into distinct levels, this method enables the development of a high-level task model and a corresponding symbolic decision policy, yielding a more efficient learning process and the capacity to generate new, symbolic skills. Furthermore, this research validates the effectiveness of this approach through empirical experiments conducted in simulated environments.

Conventional optical nonreciprocity relies on magnetic fields, light intensity, or nonlinear effects to achieve unidirectional light transmission. In contrast, a method utilizing quantum correlations for nonreciprocity is proposed, exploiting correlations between an auxiliary field and a three-level medium. This approach, based on Schrödinger picture theory, demonstrates that correlated photons can create unidirectional channels, with the degree of nonreciprocity dependent on quantum correlations, as measured by quantum discord.

We investigate the non-convex optimization issue of determining a function $f$ within a specified set $\mathcal{F}$ that minimizes the maximum $L^p$ norm of a function $g$, which is a translation of $f$ by an element from a finite set $\Lambda$. This problem is a variation of the non-convex Fenchel problem, and we study its non-convex adaptation. Our research reveals the existence of a unique, continuous, and symmetric optimal solution under certain conditions, and more is known for the case where the optimal solution is sought in the space of radial symmetric functions. Our findings are illustrated through concrete examples and further applications are discussed in the context of frame design and the problem of minimizing the maximum $L^p$ norm of a function with a band-limited function.

The CRESST experiment, which is located in Gran Sasso, Italy, is one of the most sensitive detectors of dark matter below 1 keV, utilizing $^6$Li to detect interactions between dark matter and nucleons with distinct spin-dependent properties. A new analysis of CRESST's data from Run 3B is presented, which involved 56.6 kg-years of data collection between 2014 and 2016. During this time, no signals were detected above the noise threshold, allowing for the establishment of the most stringent constraints on dark matter masses below 1 GeV, which exceed previous limits by factors of 10-100.

This research introduces a novel blind deblurring method utilizing the deblurring kernel as a mixture component. The proposed mixture, composed of Gaussian functions, can effectively approximate various deblurring kernels, including those generated by camera motion. By treating deblurring as a parameter optimization problem, the approach employs the Expectation-Maximization algorithm to yield high-accuracy kernel approximations. The obtained kernel is then used in a regularized least squares framework to efficiently solve the deblurring process. The proposed method has been shown to outperform existing blind deblurring techniques in terms of image clarity and overall performance.

This article introduces a new concept called associative BiHom-Yang-Baxter pair with weight $(r, s)$, which is a pair of matrices $(Y, B)$ satisfying specific conditions, and demonstrates its equivalence to a modified version of the Yang-Baxter equation that takes into account biHom-permutations $(r, s)$. Additionally, a new equation involving a single biHom-permutation $(r, s)$ is derived, which generalizes the bimonoidal biHom-Yang-Baxter equation.

Formal verification ensures systems meet critical requirements through the process of checking correctness. Traditional approaches separate specification from formalism, translating natural language into a formal language like Hoare logic. This paper proposes Natural Hoare Logic, integrating natural language directly into the formalism. By formalizing the syntax and semantics of Natural Hoare Logic, the approach enables the direct derivation of verification conditions from the language. This is demonstrated through the creation of a proof assistant library and its application in verifying a complex program with formal correctness guarantees.

Distributed systems face the challenge of maintaining data integrity and consistency despite node failures. To address this, the Canopus protocol was developed, which leverages the consensus of a subset of nodes to ensure data integrity. However, Canopus has a limitation in that it only handles simple failures and not more complex scenarios where nodes may malfunction in unpredictable ways. To overcome this, the RCanopus protocol was designed, which extends Canopus to deal with both basic and complex node failures. By incorporating Canopus as a building block, RCanopus enables the creation of resilient distributed applications that can withstand a wide range of node failures.

This study presents the outcomes of our research on the bending modulus of lipid bilayers composed of cholesterol and lipids, utilizing an advanced simulation technique. We discovered that the combination of cholesterol with short-tailed lipids, specifically DLPC, results in a substantial increase in the bending modulus, whereas its incorporation into other lipid compositions yields softer membranes. Cholesterol's presence in lipid bilayers significantly alters area compressibility, thickness, and curvature elasticity, thereby influencing membrane curvature.

This paper examines the loop quantum cosmological model derived from the ADM formalism, and finds that this model is equivalent to the model in [1], with outcomes that support prior research in this field.

The Pierre Auger Observatory catalog presents an unprecedented collection of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays, with energy estimates exceeding $10^{18}$ electron volts. This catalog, based on data from the observatory's first operational phase, offers a crucial examination of extreme cosmic events. This document provides an in-depth analysis of the catalog's contents, including detailed characteristics of each recorded particle, and presents an independent review of the primary findings. This review encompasses an extensive review of the primary findings, including an extensive review of the primary findings.

Deep neural networks have become the go-to choice for solving computer vision problems, including object detection. However, these networks often lack the ability to assess their prediction accuracy, which is crucial in real-world applications. Relying solely on the confidence levels of predictions can be misleading, as they tend to be overly optimistic. This paper introduces BayesOD, a Bayesian approach that incorporates uncertainty estimation into object detection. By employing Monte Carlo Dropout, BayesOD generates multiple prediction sets to estimate uncertainty. Experiments conducted on the MS COCO dataset demonstrate that BayesOD outperforms traditional object detectors in terms of accuracy and provides reliable uncertainty estimates.

The traffic forecasting problem is a crucial aspect of smart city development, with current approaches often relying on city-wide road networks. However, a more effective method is to forecast traffic on specific segments of those roads, where vehicles maintain consistent positions. To achieve this, a new framework called Traffic Forecasting on Traffic Moving Snippets (TFTOMS) has been developed. This framework involves predicting vehicle positions and speeds over a specified time frame, and our research focuses on this challenge. To address this task, we have designed a framework called the Traffic Predictor on Moving Snippets (TPoMS), which uses a combination of deep learning techniques, including convolutional neural networks and recurrent neural networks, to analyze time-series data and make accurate predictions. Our approach has been tested on two large, real-world datasets and has shown promising results, outperforming current state-of-the-art methods.

We are developing a concept of Gray rewriting, which is based on a 2-category structure, to build a 2-category of morphisms and their transformations, similar to how traditional rewriting theory forms a 2-category, but with morphism dependencies taken into account. This framework allows us to encapsulate various types of rewriting systems, including those that are context-dependent, within a single structure. By applying our theory, we can provide a unified explanation for the properties of 2-cells in both strict and non-strict monoidal categories, as well as the coherence of braided and symmetric categories.

This research introduces an innovative method for segmenting the hippocampus in MRI scans using deep learning techniques. The proposed approach combines multiple Convolutional Neural Networks, each specialized in dividing a particular region of the hippocampus into its subregions. To accomplish this, the outer and inner areas of the hippocampus are first identified using a U-Net model, after which the remaining task involves dividing the outer section into distinct subregions. To address this challenge, the method employs three Convolutional Neural Networks, each trained on a different hippocampal curvature. The selection of hippocampal curvature is based on the angle of the outer boundary, which is determined by fitting a circle to the boundary. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through quantitative evaluation on various datasets, including the subjects from the Epilepsy study and the subjects from the Alzheimer's disease study.

We investigate the transversal mode distribution in a system of non-interacting particles confined to a cylindrical container. By analyzing different non-interacting scenarios, including cylindrical symmetry and uniform boundary conditions, we reveal how the dominant transversal mode is influenced by the girth and cross-sectional area of the container. Our analysis supports the concept that a single effective quantum is sufficient for understanding the thermal properties of non-interacting systems, even in complex geometries.

Low Earth Orbits are subject to intense radiation exposure, including that experienced by astronauts. Research has revealed that certain orbital paths exhibit extremely high levels of radiation, known as South Atlantic Anomaly (SAA), which poses a significant risk to spacecraft operations. To better understand and analyze this phenomenon, this study employs a Monte Carlo simulation to model the behavior of cosmic ray alpha nuclei and protons as they become trapped within the SAA. Utilizing Geant4, a software package, the simulation tracks these particles through various interactions with matter, such as scattering, energy loss, and other nuclear reactions. The results of the simulation show that certain energy ranges are most prevalent, with secondary particles exhibiting energy levels that are lower than their primary counterparts. The study also highlights the significance of multiple particle interactions and provides insights into the complex nature of cosmic ray behavior within the SAA.

This paper introduces an innovative deep graph neural network architecture, 
comprising two main components: a pyramid-like structure that gradually reduces 
the complexity of the graph, and an intricate network that dynamically adjusts 
node connections during the training process. By combining these elements, the 
architecture effectively captures both broad and detailed patterns in complex data. 
Furthermore, it incorporates attention mechanisms to enhance its ability to learn 
robust representations, and our experiments demonstrate its superiority over other 
leading graph neural network models in various real-world tasks.

To achieve differential privacy in low-rank matrix completion, we propose the first private mechanism based on the Huber loss, which effectively balances robustness and privacy. This loss-based mechanism, particularly when employing the median of means approach, demonstrates a significant advantage over other methods in terms of both efficiency and privacy. Specifically, our differentially private Huber mechanism exhibits superior performance in the matrix noise setting, with an estimated error of O(r^2 κ^2 σ^2 n^(1/2) log^(1/2)(n) / ε n^(1/2)), which closely approaches the information-theoretic limit, up to a logarithmic factor.

We introduce The Astrodust + PAH model, a comprehensive framework for understanding interstellar dust properties, incorporating single grain size distributions, complex silicate structures, and the combined effects of small carbonaceous grains and large molecular ring structures. This model is designed to be applied to individual astronomical observations, with its parameters optimized through the OBAMAP algorithm. We demonstrate the model's capabilities on three datasets: the extinction curve of G000.0-000.0, the infrared emission spectrum of W43L, and the optical polarization measurements in the B222.0-28.2 region. Our model effectively fits these datasets, accurately reproducing the secondary extinction peak, infrared emission features, and polarization measurements. This unified approach provides a consistent explanation for the extinction, emission, and polarization phenomena associated with interstellar dust.

The formation of low-mass stars and their surrounding disks is still not fully understood. Observations of young low-mass stars and their disks are essential in understanding the process. CIDA 1, a low-mass star, has an unusual disk structure that is being shaped by a large planet. Using ALMA, we analyzed the disk's composition and found it to be asymmetric, with the majority of the material on one side. This is likely due to a large planet interacting with the disk. Our analysis indicates that the planet has a mass similar to Jupiter and orbits at a distance of about 100 astronomical units from the star. This discovery provides new insights into the process of planet formation and migration in low-mass star systems.

We introduce and analyze the "Most Clicks" Lights Out problem, which involves determining the maximum number of clicks needed to turn off all the lights in various configurations. This problem is solved and proven to be linear for grid-based initial setups of any size. Additionally, we investigate 'Grid with a Hole' and 'Frogs and Toads' variations of the problem.

This paper introduces a novel, multi-step variational model for image segmentation that integrates image restoration capabilities. The model is structured into two interconnected components: a data-fidelity step focused on restoring image details and a segmentation step that leverages the enhanced image to refine segmentation. The first component employs a non-local mean filter to mitigate noise and over-smoothing, whereas the latter step utilizes a regularized Chan-Vese model with a data-driven constraint that incorporates information from the enhanced image. By alternating between these steps, the proposed model achieves superior segmentation results. Our approach demonstrates robust performance on a variety of image types, including color and grayscale, as well as different types of distortions such as corruption, artifacts, and missing data.

Program analysis through Abstract Interpretation involves simulating the behavior of a program to identify potential errors, but the process is often hindered by a significant computational cost that arises when ascending and descending phases are combined. To address this issue, a new cost model has been developed to isolate and separate these two phases, enabling the creation of tailored strategies to optimize each. The proposed model is then applied to a specific scenario where it successfully reduces the computational cost of ascending phases by a factor of 1000 and descending phases by a factor of 10.

Our research reveals that topological phonons in BiFeO3 exhibit percolation characteristics, and these features can be controlled and modified by applying and manipulating light. By utilizing terahertz pulses, we can induce a phase transition from a non-centrosymmetric A-type antiferroelectric state to a paraelectric state, and our findings demonstrate that this process results in the disappearance of Weyl phonons and the emergence of Rayleigh modes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that optical excitation can be used to control the topological properties of phonons, and this control is observed through time-resolved neutron scattering experiments.

Unsupervised outlier detection in various fields has become an increasingly important task due to the growth of data volumes.  A widely used method for this task relies on computing pairwise distances between all data points.  To address this computationally intensive problem, researchers have developed techniques to avoid computing all distances by utilizing data structures.  However, these approaches often compromise on detection accuracy.  In this research, a novel method is proposed that achieves both high accuracy and efficiency by analyzing the local density of points.  This approach builds a weighted graph representing the proximity of points and identifies outliers by detecting isolated vertices.  To address the computational complexity of this method, a novel algorithm is proposed that processes the degree sequence of vertices in parallel.  Experimental evaluations demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms existing solutions in terms of speed while maintaining comparable or superior accuracy.

The movement of a thin reflective barrier alters the dynamics of an atom located perpendicular to it, held in place by an external force. This motion induces a non-zero probability of the atom being in an excited state, and the emitted radiation it produces can be calculated. Our analysis reveals that the atom's excitation and emitted radiation are amplified when the barrier accelerates rapidly, and this effect intensifies as the acceleration increases exponentially with the logarithm of the acceleration parameter. Additionally, our study shows that the atom's excitation probability and emitted radiation vary differently depending on whether they are evaluated in the laboratory frame or the transformed frame associated with the barrier's movement.

Machine learning tasks often rely on graph representations, yet they can be
unfair to specific subgroups within these representations. To ensure equitable
treatment of these subgroups, we propose a method for learning fair graph
representations by incorporating fairness constraints into a graph embedding
problem. Our novel approach, called Localized Neighborhood Fairness (LNF), aims
to achieve fairness within the immediate surroundings of each data point while
preserving the overall graph structure. By framing fairness as hypergeometric
constraints, we can leverage existing graph embedding methods to learn fair
graphs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments
on both simulated and real-world data, showcasing its ability to produce
meaningful graph representations.

This research focuses on developing a method to approximate solutions for the kinetic equation describing a reversible enzymatic reaction. By employing an analytical technique, we can systematically derive increasingly accurate approximations of the reaction dynamics over time. We demonstrate that each iteration yields a more precise solution, with notable improvements over earlier methods. Our analysis reveals that each successive iteration effectively reduces a specific type of error, namely enzyme-related error, thereby enhancing the solution's accuracy.

Researchers have conducted an examination of the LHC's 13 TeV data, encompassing 36.1 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collisions, in search of specific patterns indicative of supersymmetry. By analyzing events featuring numerous jets and momentum loss, the study targets the decay of lightest neutralinos into lighter states. Split and natural supersymmetry models are among the theoretical frameworks considered, with focus given to chargino and gluino production. According to the standard model, no statistically significant discrepancies were found, with results consistent with expected outcomes. Specifically, supersymmetry production scenarios were constrained, including chargino and gluino masses up to 1.2 TeV in split SUSY and up to 800 GeV in natural SUSY.

To identify and analyze rational expectations financial bubbles, a new approach is proposed, utilizing a stochastic model with a mean-reverting process for the time it takes for a bubble to burst. The model's key parameter is estimated by analyzing the relationship between a stock's returns and its fundamental value, after adjusting for the stock's fundamental value and the estimated time a bubble will last. The method is validated through simulations and applied to actual stock market data, demonstrating its effectiveness in detecting and analyzing financial bubbles.

Quantum harmonic oscillators are fundamental in various physical fields, and their behavior in equilibrium and non-equilibrium states is extensively studied. The temporal dynamics of these systems are typically analyzed through path integral methods, which are well-suited for equilibrium states but become complicated when driven out of equilibrium. This work demonstrates the application of Monte Carlo techniques to simulate the quantum harmonic oscillator's behavior, and their potential utility in solving complex many-body problems.

Recent research has shown that incorporating review text into recommender systems can significantly improve their performance. However, most existing methods treat all reviews equally, disregarding the crucial aspect of their sentiment. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel Sentiment-aware Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN) that leverages the sentiment of reviews to provide more accurate recommendations. The proposed model consists of two main components: a sentiment-aware item representation network and a review-based recommendation network. The former captures the essential information of items by integrating their implicit characteristics and the sentiments expressed in their reviews, while the latter utilizes reviews to predict an item's rating and the user's likelihood of purchasing it. Through experiments on two real-world datasets, we have demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach, which significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of both review-based and sentiment-recovery performance evaluations.

This research explores the feasibility of employing code-switching transformation (CST) as a data augmentation method for Arabic-English code-switched text. Our study compares the effectiveness of three types of lexical replacement models in CST: deep contextual models, non-contextual models, and benchmark monolingual models. We evaluate the quality of CST using two metrics: switch-accuracy and switch-edit. Our results indicate that deep contextual models outperform the other models, with accuracy results suggesting that contextual models are capable of accurately identifying code-switched words. On the other hand, edit results reveal that non-contextual models are more efficient, requiring fewer edits to perform CST.

We demonstrate that the groups of surface homeomorphisms acting on compact surfaces, excluding the sphere and surface of infinite genus, are not non-compact when using the supremum metric, and for surfaces of non-Euclidean genus, any closed subgroup is also non-compact under the supremum metric, except for surface group actions.

We investigate integrable branes within the context of generalized lambda deformations. Initially, we rederive the brane brane scattering symmetry in the framework of the lambda deformation, followed by an in-depth examination of branes with affine $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ symmetry. We derive the brane brane scattering symmetry for this specific case and explore the properties of these branes, including their relation to S-duals of lambda deformation and their connection to WZW deformations in the undeformed limit. Furthermore, we explore the possibility of constructing conformal field theories with two such branes.

This study introduces a new, efficient method for automatically correcting twisted triangles in hexahedral meshes, a common issue in complicated areas of such meshes. The proposed algorithm, based on graph theory, identifies the simplest structure to address the problem and then utilizes an existing solution to resolve the twisted triangles. The algorithm's performance was tested on a comprehensive set of 1,000 randomly generated mesh configurations, with impressive results, averaging 58.12 corrected triangles per hexahedron, or a maximum of 58.88 corrected triangles in the most complex case.

The task of relation extraction involves utilizing text to establish connections between entities and their attributes. A critical challenge in this process is distinguishing between a entity pair's existing connections and those that are missing from a pre-existing knowledge graph. We propose the KGLNEX framework, which addresses this issue by integrating knowledge graph link prediction to enhance relation classification accuracy. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach yields improved results on four distinct datasets compared to traditional relational extraction methods.

This study introduces a novel analytical delay model for CMOS circuits, developed using the Curve Fitting Toolbox in Matlab. The proposed model offers a more precise and versatile alternative to traditional parameterized models, which often rely on approximations and can be supplanted by parameterless models tailored to specific technologies or even individual transistors. Although parameterized models are computationally efficient, the introduced model strikes a balance between accuracy and speed, as it minimizes the number of required parameters. The method involves creating a custom function that maps a chosen delay metric to the critical dimensions of the transistern, followed by the utilization of the Curve Fitting Toolbox to derive a custom analytical function. The resulting model can be seamlessly integrated into SPICE simulations, enabling the calculation of analytical delay models for complex CMOS circuits.

We propose a novel framework for measuring the smoothness of a metric space, allowing for granular control over state transitions in reinforcement learning. Our framework is versatile and can be applied to complex, high-dimensional state spaces by defining smoothness metrics tailored to specific domains. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach across various complex state spaces, including those involving robotic manipulation and navigation.

Studies have shown that the way living things are grouped together animacy is also reflected in the way the brain processes visual information, and it also helps explain the way the brain recognizes faces and categorizes objects. This research introduces an innovative approach to filter multidimensional linear and nonlinear simulation data, with a focus on preserving structures within complex systems. A novel convex optimization-based filter is developed to tackle the challenge of maintaining the accuracy and reliability of simulation data, particularly in the context of multi-dimensional nonlinear systems. The proposed method is evaluated through a series of tests on both artificial and real-world simulation data, demonstrating its effectiveness in a range of scenarios, including the simulation of physical phenomena such as fluid dynamics and magnetohydrodynamics.

Quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) in X-ray binaries have been observed to change in frequency over time, which has been linked to variations in the accretion disk's inner edge. Observations of the black hole binary system MAXI J1535-571 have shown a decrease in QPO frequency during its outburst, which has been interpreted as evidence for an increase in the distance of the accretion disk's inner edge from the black hole. A new analysis of the system's 2018 outburst using data from the Insight-HXMT observatory has revealed a significant change in the system's behavior, which is now understood as a result of the system transitioning from a type-I to a type-C QPO state. A detailed study of the system's evolution during this outburst has revealed that the system's light curve and spectral properties underwent significant changes, which have been linked to the system transitioning between different states. A new analysis of the system's light curve has revealed that the system's quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) were present in the system's light curve for a significant portion of the system's outburst, which has been linked to the system transitioning from a hard state to a soft state. A new analysis of the system's spectral properties has revealed that the system's spectral properties varied significantly over the course of the system's outburst, which has been linked to the system transitioning between different states. A key factor in achieving success in multi-agent reinforcement learning is the ability to transfer knowledge from one task to another. To address this challenge, we propose a new approach called Transfer Empowerment, which utilizes a social intrinsic motivation to guide agents in learning transferable skills. This method focuses on acquiring actions that enable agents to consistently respond to each other's behaviors, thereby increasing predictability and reducing uncertainty in interactions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a new set of cooperative tasks, showing that it successfully learns transferable skills and outperforms a baseline method of transfer learning.

We introduce a novel recognition system that can identify virtually any material when presented with an unknown scene, using only two reference images per material. By leveraging existing material databases, our training process is fully unsupervised, and our system is evaluated on real-world benchmarks, demonstrating its exceptional performance.

This article provides a comprehensive overview of Lie 2-algebras, beginning with an in-depth examination of their unique properties and structural components. Key points include the derivation of their definition and essential criteria. The article then delves into the classification and essential requirements of Lie 2-algebras. Furthermore, it explores how Lie 2-algebras arise from specific types of Lie groups and their respective higher components, with a focus on nilpotent Lie groups. The relationship between Lie 2-algebras and 2-Lie algebras is also discussed. The article then shifts its attention to Lie 2-algebras that are derived from Lie 3-algebras and their respective 2-Lie algebras. The article then examines how Lie 2-algebras can be constructed from Lie groups and their respective extensions, with a focus on central extensions. The article then discusses how Lie 2-algebras can be used to study Lie group extensions, with a focus on central extensions.
