We introduce a novel approach for local feature matching, LoFTR, which is
a transformer-based method that directly maps pixel-to-pixel relationships in
image pairs containing keypoints and descriptors. Unlike previous methods that
relied on detecting features, LoFTR takes raw images as input and produces a
matching descriptor that guides the discovery of keypoints and descriptors.
Diving into the geometric underpinnings of feature matching, we develop a
detector-free description learning framework, where LoFTR's description encodes
a description map that maps keypoints and descriptors across different feature
pyramids. Furthermore, we find that self-attention in transformers is naturally
aligned with matching descriptors' geometric properties, and propose a detector-
free transformer model to learn description maps. Experiments demonstrate that
our method outperforms state-of-the-art methods, with matching descriptors that
can be directly used for various tasks, such as image registration and 3D
reconstruction.

The vector magnetic field measurements of the sun's atmosphere are crucial for understanding solar activity and space weather, but they are limited by the inherent constraints of the instruments used. To overcome these limitations, various inversion methods have been developed to infer full magnetic field information from limited line-of-sight intensity and Stokes $Q$ and $U$ polarizations data. However, these inversion methods can introduce biases into the derived horizontal field components. This study aims to identify and address these biases by analyzing and comparing the performance of four inversion methods using synthetic data and real observations. The results indicate that these biases can significantly affect the interpretation of magnetic field data, particularly in the sun's penumbra regions. To mitigate these biases, the study proposes a novel approach that involves analyzing the distribution of magnetic field angles and comparing them with the distribution of line-of-sight polarization. This approach has been shown to be effective in identifying and correcting biases in the derived horizontal field components.

This research introduces a novel game-theoretic framework for managing autonomous demand side using a dynamic billing approach. The utility company implements an instantaneous billing policy that charges consumers based on their real-time energy usage. To effectively manage their energy consumption, consumers develop schedules that minimize their overall energy costs. In a proposed aggregative game model, each consumer aims to find an optimal solution that balances their energy costs against comfort preferences. The framework's convergence and stability are rigorously proven, and simulation results validate its practical effectiveness.

The unification of quantum and general theories of gravity remains a fundamental challenge in modern physics.  One promising approach to address this issue is through the use of modified gravity theories, which have garnered significant attention in recent years.  The so-called Rastall gravity, a specific type of modified theory, has been extensively studied in the literature.  In this study, we investigate the gravitational influence on heat loss from an electrically charged black hole in the context of Rastall theory, a scenario that is relevant to astrophysical black holes.  By employing a specific coordinate system, we derive a line element that is characteristic of Rastall theory.  Furthermore, we investigate the thermodynamic properties of this black hole, including its surface area, temperature, and entropy, and analyze how these quantities are affected by the presence of additional Rastall parameters.  Our results reveal that black holes in Rastall theory exhibit a more complex behavior than their general relativistic counterparts, with the gravitational influence on heat loss being significantly altered.

The results demonstrate that the power-law spectral distribution of a unitary operator U can lead to convergence rate convergence in the von Neumann ergodic theorem, specifically with a rate of $n^{-\alpha/p}$ for some $\alpha > 0$ and $p > 0$. This is achieved without any assumptions on multiplicity, and it is shown that even in cases of infinite multiplicity, such as a rotation with irrational angle $\theta$ on the interval $[0,1]$, a power-law spectral distribution can facilitate a polynomial convergence rate in the ergodic theorem.

The Gaia mission's photometric spectra can be utilized to identify metal-poor stars, which are crucial for understanding the Milky Way's formation and evolution. We developed a method to detect metal-poor stars by leveraging the line blanketing effect in the line-rich region of the Gaia BP/RP spectra. By comparing the flux differences between the line-rich and line-free regions, we developed an indicator F to distinguish between metal-poor and metal-rich stars. By analyzing the 2 million Gaia Early Data Release 3 stars with full spectra, we found that the F distribution shows a clear metal-poor excess. By setting a suitable threshold, we identified approximately 10,000 metal-poor stars, with a high purity rate of around 90%. Furthermore, we determined the metal-poor stars' average metallicity to be approximately [Fe/H] = -1.0 dex, with a standard deviation of 0.5 dex. By cross-referencing with external metallicity data, we found a strong correlation between the F and [Fe/H], and established a metallicity estimation formula. By analyzing the spatial distribution of the identified metal-poor stars, we discovered a significant concentration in the Galactic bulge and disk, and found that the disk's radial metallicity gradient is approximately -0.07 dex/kpc.

Wildfires have become a pressing concern in the US, particularly during the dry summer months. The devastation caused by these fires is extensive, resulting in the loss of property, infrastructure, and even human lives. The increasing frequency and intensity of wildfires are attributed to a combination of factors, including prolonged droughts, high temperatures, and human activities. The US National Interagency Fire Center (NIFC) has developed the National Fire Danger Rating System (NFDRS) to assess fire danger and predict potential outcomes. This analysis utilizes the NIFC's NFDRS data to create a new severity index, which measures the intensity of wildfires across the US. The index is calculated using a combination of fire size and duration, and its values are analyzed to identify trends and correlations with climate indicators. The results show that the index correlates strongly with climate indicators, including temperature and precipitation, and can be used to predict future wildfire severity.

The effectiveness of quantitative methods in historical linguistics relies heavily on the accuracy of their underlying assumptions.  In the case of corpus-based measures, it is crucial to confirm that variations in these metrics truly represent changes in language structure.  This study aims to validate the measurement of morphological complexity by examining whether alterations in related linguistic features align with anticipated trends.  Using the English language as a reference, the authors analyze the development of three specific features - grammaticalization, lexical richness, and morpheme frequency - across different time periods.  By correlating these features with established metrics like the Type-Token-Distance (TTD), the researchers demonstrate that the selected complexity measures are capable of accurately tracking changes in language structure.  Moreover, the results indicate that the English language has undergone a significant increase in morphological complexity over time, primarily due to the emergence of function words.  This finding challenges the long-held belief that morphological complexity has consistently decreased throughout language evolution.

Galaxy cluster research has revealed small-scale gravitational lens effects that contradict predictions based on cold dark matter models. Self-interacting dark matter was proposed to resolve this discrepancy, with studies showing that self-interactions can significantly alter the dark matter density distribution in galaxy clusters. This paper investigates how these interactions impact the dark energy density distribution and the resulting gravitational lensing in galaxy clusters. Utilizing a modified code, we simulate dark matter density profiles in galaxy clusters with varying degrees of self-interaction, taking into account dark matter and dark energy interactions. Our analysis reveals that self-interactions can substantially modify the dark matter density, with the effect becoming more pronounced as the equation of state parameter approaches -1. This has implications for understanding the dark sector interactions and the ultimate fate of the universe.

We develop techniques for decreasing the complexity of differential equations 
when the system's full state cannot be observed. These methods enable the 
accurate reconstruction of key system characteristics based on limited data. 
Our approach includes deriving a reduced model from a discrete-time snapshot 
envelope obtained from simulation data. Additionally, we establish a 
mathematical link between the continuous and discrete models. A model 
reduction algorithm is then applied to generate a low-dimensional discrete model, 
which is used to create a continuous model that preserves essential system 
characteristics. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated using the 
Cerebellar Ataxia Virus model, a system modeling a disease's spread.

This research introduces the m-arithmetic mean-based fast independent component analysis (m-ar-K-FICA) method, a novel approach for blind source separation. The m-arithmetic mean is a robust measure resistant to outliers, making it a reliable estimator in data analysis. Our work demonstrates that the m-ar-K-FICA can efficiently recover independent sources by maximizing the arithmetic mean of the order statistics of absolute data values. The Fast ICA algorithm leverages the derivative of the M-estimator to accelerate convergence. Our simulation results show that the m-ar-K-FICA outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and resistance to outliers.

This study introduces a novel method for identifying social media events unfolding across various geographic locations and timeframes in real-time. By leveraging the dynamic nature of social media events, the proposed approach models multi-scale dependency patterns among events occurring in different regions and time intervals. Furthermore, the sparsity of data is addressed by incorporating a non-negative tensor factorization technique, which factorizes a data tensor representing event occurrences. Each event is characterized by its underlying activity patterns, spatial distribution, and chronological progression. By integrating spatial and temporal information, the system effectively captures diverse event types, such as festivals, sports competitions, and cultural gatherings.

We establish the optimal Lipschitz regularity for solutions to the equation
$-\mathrm{div} (A(x,\nabla u)) = \delta_{\Gamma}$
within a bounded domain $\Omega$ in the $n$-dimensional space. Here, $\Gamma$ is a hypersurface and $\delta_{\Gamma}$ represents a surface Dirac measure. The equation's coefficients are linearly growth bounded and satisfy specific conditions related to integrability and anisotropy. The results of this study enable the use of measures in action as a limiting case of the $p$-Laplace problem.

To identify novel cobalt-rich materials with potential for advanced applications, researchers employed computational methods to explore the yttrium-cobalt-boron system. By using evolutionary search, they discovered a total of 13 new cobalt-dominant Y-Co-B compounds, 12 of which exhibit stable structures. These stable compounds feature unique characteristics such as high cobalt content and high magnetic properties. Additionally, the researchers found that certain Y-Co-B compounds possess exceptional mechanical properties and thermal conductivity, making them potential candidates for use in advanced magnetic and structural applications.

In the field of display advertising, risk management and budget constraint are pressing issues that real-world bidding systems face. To address these challenges, we have developed an innovative adaptive auction-based risk metric and risk-aware bidding strategy that takes risk and budget into consideration simultaneously. We leverage the correlation between different risk metrics and the click-through rate to create a dynamic adaptive risk metric. Furthermore, we have modified the bidding strategy to incorporate both risk and budget constraints, ensuring that the risk and budget are optimized. Our proposed strategy is validated through both theoretical analysis and experimental evaluation, demonstrating its effectiveness in satisfying the risk and budget constraints while maximizing expected revenue.

Non-classical resources in quantum mechanics are crucial for various applications, including quantum computation and communication. One key resource is quantum non-classicality, which can be demonstrated through the concept of quantum steering. Research has shown a strong connection between quantum non-classicality and the inability of certain variables to be described by a classical probabilistic model, known as a joint probability distribution. Specifically, the presence of quantum non-classicality can be confirmed when attempting to construct such a model, leading to violations of certain inequalities. However, the relationship between this construction and the negativity of the Wigner function remains unclear. In this study, we explore this relationship, revealing that when attempting to create a Wigner function from a quantum state, if such a model is impossible, the resulting function will exhibit negativity. This finding provides further insight into the connection between quantum non-classicality and the negativity of Wigner functions.

The typical security analysis of quantum key distribution assumes a uniformly distributed random seed for privacy amplification. However, in practice, the random seed is often generated by a preceding random number generator, which may produce non-uniform output. This study investigates the impact of non-uniform input on the security of quantum key distribution, using two specific approaches to model the random number generator: a uniform distribution and a discrete Gaussian distribution. It is demonstrated that the key distillation rate is not necessarily reduced when the random number generator produces non-uniform output, and in some cases, the rate can be higher than in the case of a uniformly distributed seed. This research provides new insights into the use of non-uniform random seeds in privacy amplification, and its findings are expected to be of significant value for the development of practical quantum key distribution systems.

This research paper focuses on a specific type of curve, known as a time-like Bertrand curve, within a four-dimensional Euclidean space. It derives the mathematical condition that must be met for such a curve to exist and identifies two distinct categories based on this condition. Furthermore, the study presents concrete examples to illustrate both categories.

We analyze the behavior of coalescing particles governed by Feller diffusion equations, considering various initial configurations. Our research yields precise results for key metrics, including particle collision times and final positions, as well as the distribution of sampled particles. These analytical findings are particularly significant for population genetics applications. To support these analyses, our work incorporates detailed mathematical derivations and complementary numerical simulations.

In this study, we present a diagrammatic method for analyzing multi-photon scattering in waveguide QED systems. We introduce a systematic approach to creating diagrams that represent multi-photon scattering amplitudes in complex systems involving multiple atoms and complex energy structures. We establish a set of basic rules to build the scattering matrix using these diagrams, which we then use to derive the correct scattering matrix for a variety of configurations. We also demonstrate the application of this method by calculating key features of multi-photon scattering, such as transmission and absorption probabilities, in a many-body system of waveguide-coupled atoms.

The phenomenon of Boosted Dark Matter, where dark matter interacts with visible matter to create observable signals, is being studied through various detection methods. A new study examines how spin-dependent interactions affect the dark matter's impact on visible matter, focusing on the differences between interactions with light and hard scattering. The research reveals that light scattering, previously overlooked, can account for a significant portion of signals in some detection methods, particularly when spin-dependent interactions are involved. The study also identifies the optimal mass and flux of dark matter for spin-dependent interactions to occur, suggesting that future research should consider this type of interaction more carefully.
This note employs Faulhaber's Formula to elucidate why odd Bernoulli numbers equate to zero.

Continuous phase modulation (CPM) is a promising technique for next-generation wireless communication systems due to its robustness against phase errors and channel distortions, as well as its ability to be seamlessly integrated with existing systems. The standard approach to demodulating CPM signals involves the conventional differential detection (CDD) method, which is characterized by its simplicity and low computational requirements. However, the delay inherent in CPM detection is a significant concern, as it is directly proportional to the signal's transmission time. This paper explores the optimization of CPM detection using conventional differential detection, focusing on minimizing detection delay. The proposed solutions involve selecting specific CPM parameters to reduce delay, as well as developing a novel non-coherent differential detection scheme that achieves the same level of performance with significantly reduced delay. The results demonstrate that the new detection method can achieve substantial delay reductions of up to 50% for certain CPM parameters, while maintaining the same bit error rate performance as the conventional method.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning is to segment a vast state-action space into compact clusters, then learn the reward function solely from these clusters. However, manually labeling these clusters is labor-intensive and often impractical. To address this, we propose an innovative approach that leverages visual feedback to automatically organize clusters into sub-groups, thereby significantly reducing the labeling effort. By organizing these visual clusters, our method simplifies the labeling process and enhances the overall reward learning efficiency.

Using the noncommutative pencil model, this study examines the parton distribution functions in nucleons within noncommutative space-time. The calculations are based on the noncommutative nucleon's forward scattering amplitude and its relation to the proton's distribution function. The findings reveal that noncommutativity affects the proton's momentum and Moliere distribution. The distribution function $f_p(x)$ is influenced by the noncommutativity parameter $\theta$, particularly when $x$ approaches 1. The research also discusses how the proton's Moliere radius is related to the noncommutativity parameter $\theta$.

In typical topological systems, the boundary is characterized by a specific number of edge states, which is directly related to the topological invariant. However, in models with frustration, this relationship is disrupted, enabling the emergence of a one-dimensional topological phase bounded by a line defect. A key example of this is the frustrated Toric code, featuring a Majorana zero mode at the vertex where the line originates. This phenomenon can be understood through a modified version of the Kane-Lee string operator, which exhibits non-trivial behavior at the string's endpoints due to frustration.

We establish the first- and second-order eigenvalue statistics for the Gaussian GOE band matrices following an perturbation from a low-rank Hermitian matrix. Our findings confirm and expand upon previous work, revealing that the statistics of the perturbed band matrix are governed by the same non-linear sigma model that describes the behavior of large random matrices with band structures. This confirms a hypothesis proposed by Erdos, Yau, and Zhang in their 2021 study.

Recent advances in dialogue systems have been driven by the adoption of pre-trained language models, which have achieved superior performance in various tasks. However, recent studies suggest that general-purpose models may not be optimal for the dialogue domain, which is characterized by unique semantic and pragmatic features. To bridge this gap, this research introduces SemDialog, a novel pre-training strategy tailored to enhance the performance of dialogue systems. By introducing specific objectives, SemDialog leverages semantic context and exploits the relationships between semantic units, thereby pre-training models with more relevant and effective information. Experimental results demonstrate that SemDialog significantly outperforms existing pre-training methods across various dialogue understanding tasks.

In the rapidly evolving field of artificial intelligence, there's an increasing need to assess the understandability of algorithms. This study aims to develop a new framework for measuring interpretability, which is grounded in cognitive science principles. By analyzing the knowledge structures of humans, we can gauge the complexity of an algorithm based on how easily it can be learned by humans. This framework is built upon a cognitive hierarchy model and uses a neural network to simulate human learning. The framework allows for the creation of a measurable and quantifiable interpretability metric, which is validated through experiments involving human participants. This new approach to interpretability is an essential step towards improving the transparency and trustworthiness of AI systems.

Anomaly detection is a critical task in various applications, particularly in detecting irregularities. The unsupervised anomaly detection method, Isolation Forest (iForest), is efficient and effective, but its performance is often hindered by its inability to utilize additional information. To address this limitation, we have developed a weakly supervised variant of iForest, referred to as TiWS-iForest, which integrates iForest with simple local classifiers in a hierarchical structure. The proposed method is efficient, effective, and robust, as demonstrated by its superior performance on synthetic and real-world datasets, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods.

A novel Bayesian estimation method for extreme value theory is proposed, which utilizes a Poisson process representation. This approach decomposes the data into an unknown number of clusters, with each cluster's height measured in units of the distribution function, resulting in a more intuitive model. This model's simplicity and transparency facilitate the adoption of widely used statistical techniques, such as the sum of squares, for the first time. Consequently, the integration of Bayesian and frequentist methodologies becomes achievable. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the clustering approach yields estimates comparable to traditional Bayesian methods.

This study explores areas where average cross-sectional values remain constant, consistent with the Efimov effect's predictions. To achieve this, we developed a cross-sectional formula based on the distance between three particles. By applying it to the wave function produced through three-body scattering, our analysis indicates that cross-sectional values will decrease asymptotically as the energy approaches zero, contradicting the predictions of Efimov theory.

This paper presents COMET-ATOMIC 2020, a massive, directed, and weighted knowledge graph called ATOMIC 2020, which is specifically designed for tasks requiring commonsense understanding. This paper outlines the characteristics of the dataset, its underlying principles, and methods used to evaluate it.

The Hi-GAL survey is a large-scale study of young star-forming regions across the Milky Way's central area, focusing on specific wavelength ranges. To support this investigation, the survey team created a data processing system that utilizes software based on the GILDAR pipeline, incorporating modifications to accommodate the unique capabilities of the Herschel Space Observatory. The team then applied this data processing system to the survey's complete dataset, resulting in maps and spectral images for all observations. To verify the effectiveness of this system, the team conducted thorough examinations of the data, including checks on the signal-to-noise ratio, and identified instances of instrumental issues. Ultimately, the processed data and corresponding analysis are available for public access.

The presence of a metallicity variation within the first population of NGC 2808 has been thoroughly examined through a comprehensive analysis of high-resolution spectra. By utilizing the UVES spectrograph, we obtained detailed spectra of 14 blue stars, which are believed to be the oldest within the globular cluster. By cross-referencing our findings with previous studies, we have established a reliable set of data for the cluster's metallicity variations. Our results reveal a significant metallicity spread of 0.14 dex, which is consistent with previous observations. Moreover, we have established a direct correlation between the abundance of nitrogen and the metallicity spread within the cluster. This relationship is further supported by our findings that a larger metallicity spread within NGC 2808 is associated with a larger nitrogen abundance spread. Our research provides new insights into the complex formation history of NGC 2808.

To analyze single file diffusion, we consider particles confined within a confined space. The particles' movement is restricted, preventing them from passing each other. Our study focuses on the movement of a central particle in a long, straight tube. The particle's exit time statistics are derived using an entropy-based approach, taking into account its entropic forces. Our analysis reveals that the exit time and related statistics can be accurately described by an exponential distribution. Our findings also show that the particle's mean square displacement follows single file diffusion behavior. Our statistical model is validated through Monte Carlo simulations.

The issue of quantum measurement inconsistency is resolved by reinterpreping the event spaces associated with different Meissner operators, which are responsible for different types of quantum measurements. By applying the quantum formulation of Bayes' rule, we demonstrate that the event spaces corresponding to Meissner operators are indeed equivalent, thereby establishing consistency in the probabilistic framework governing quantum measurements.

We've developed a novel method to establish the initial conditions for Small System Effects (SSE) in heavy ion collisions. This approach involves solving the Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) Equation of State (EoS) across the entire phase diagram, which we then use to generate a detailed chart of ionization probabilities as functions of temperature and transverse flow as a function of the number of constituents. This method enables us to accurately reproduce the characteristics of observed data from the LHC, which in turn allows us to determine the constituent multiplicity and the point of quark coalescence.

In 1953, Milnor characterized the structure of the Steenrod algebra and its dual via a specific basis in a particular form. Building on this, this paper presents a formula for each non-trivial element in a particular module of a restricted Lie algebra dual to the Steenrod algebra at prime $p \geq 3$. This result enables the identification of key properties of the Lie algebra, including the maximum element weight in the ad-nilpotent basis and the number of its non-trivial cohomology classes in top-dimensional space.

Astronomers have long been interested in using the Lyman ultraviolet (LyUV) range to study interstellar gas and star formation, but traditional methods have been hindered by the lack of suitable detectors and the need to filter out harmful light from the Sun and Earth. A new approach involves employing Lyman-alpha emission from specific planetary orbits to observe LyUV wavelengths, but this requires the development of advanced filtering technology. We have designed and built a prototype Lyman-alpha interference filter that has been thoroughly tested and has shown promising results, with a measured full-width half-maximum of 5.3 Angstroms and a peak transmission rate of approximately 10 percent. The filter's performance has been evaluated through both laboratory and simulated space environment testing, demonstrating its potential to significantly advance future space-based missions.

This study investigates distributed control strategies for interconnected linear systems that exhibit specific symmetries, leading to a decentralized controller design that leverages graphs to handle multiple inputs and outputs simultaneously. Graphs are used to determine system connections and suggest feasible subspace projections for local controllers to achieve optimal control in a distributed manner. By representing the interconnected systems as a tensor product of matrices and a graph adjacency matrix, we derive a unified framework to design the optimal local controllers as adaptive graph signals and corresponding graph filters. This approach is illustrated with an example of interconnected triple masses connected via springs, where an optimal graph filter is designed to achieve a specified target configuration.

Image retrieval systems that employ large, manually curated databases of keywords and visual representations can be significantly enhanced by integrating user input.  Current active indexing methods rely on a single query to determine suitable tags and corresponding images, limiting their effectiveness due to the inherent ambiguity and complexity of natural language queries.  To overcome these limitations, we propose an active indexing framework that leverages multiple user queries to continuously refine its understanding and adapt to diverse query types.  By employing a graph-based model, our approach enables the simultaneous processing of multiple queries and incorporates user feedback to optimize its performance.  Moreover, our system leverages inter-query relationships to improve its efficiency and adaptability.  Our proposed method demonstrates superior performance compared to existing techniques on a comprehensive image dataset.

This study presents a secure communication method that operates effectively in environments with significant noise, requiring only the shared secret key derived from noise itself. The proposed technique is versatile and can be applied to various modulation methods. It is demonstrated that the proposed method is equivalent to traditional key-based communication when using Gaussian noise and QAM, and exhibits superior performance in scenarios involving non-Gaussian noise, such as impulsive noise, with a shared key consisting of 100 bits.

A theoretical model is developed to investigate the movement of particles in complex potentials that have intricate shapes. This model incorporates the effects of dispersion and uses the concept of generalized Brownian motion to describe transport in systems with barriers of varying periods and heights. The model's implications are explored in a system resembling a mechanical structure, and its impact on the flow of particles through such a system is analyzed in terms of its current and speed.

This paper presents an innovative approach to locally projecting impulse responses, allowing for more adaptable estimation. Our technique, which combines elements of nonparametric regression, enhances the precision of initial impulse response estimates. We demonstrate that our method can accurately mimic the performance of locally projected OLS under specific conditions, while also providing a statistical framework for evaluating various features of these responses. The efficacy of this nonparametrically projected local regression is validated through simulation tests and an empirical analysis of shock responses in the U.S.

We investigate the influence of the electromagnetic quantum vacuum on the angular momentum of the fundamental particle. By considering the Landau model of a particle in a uniform magnetic field, we calculate the angular Casimir momentum resulting from high-frequency vacuum fluctuations. The outcome shows that this angular momentum is non-zero and is directly proportional to the particle's charge and the applied magnetic field. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this angular momentum is independent of the specific shape of the fundamental cell used for boundary condition imposition.

The task of fine-grained named entity typing (FGET) is a crucial challenge in natural language processing, which involves classifying entities into more specific subcategories. A proposed solution, FGNET-RH, is a novel framework that leverages a geometric structure known as hyperbolic space to improve entity classification. By utilizing hyperbolic space, FGNET-RH can more effectively capture the inherent hierarchical relationships between entities, which is often overlooked in traditional methods. An entity classification model is first proposed, which is then refined through a dynamic adjustment process that further enhances its ability to distinguish between entities. Comprehensive evaluations on diverse datasets have shown that FGNET-RH consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.
This paper establishes upper limits on the second Hankel determinant for functions within the class $\mathcal{U}$ and a more general class $\mathcal{S}$.

As demand for computing resources grows, particularly in areas like scientific research, businesses, and entertainment, cloud data centers are becoming increasingly vital in meeting these needs. However, the workload on these resources can be unpredictable, making it difficult to efficiently utilize available virtual machines. In response to this issue, a novel approach called Prepartition has been developed to dynamically adjust the workload on cloud resources. By dividing cloud servers into smaller units and redistributing tasks among them, Prepartition aims to minimize overhead on virtual machines, thereby improving overall performance.

In game theory, predicting equilibrium outcomes is crucial for forecasting the results of strategic interactions. However, the complexity of games often makes it challenging to determine their equilibria, particularly in dynamic settings. This paper proposes the use of Fixed Point Networks (FPNs), which can learn to predict the equilibria of both static and dynamic games, including those with multiple and continuous action spaces. FPNs are versatile and can accommodate various game types, including stochastic and partially observable dynamics. Experimental results demonstrate that FPNs can accurately predict the equilibria of diverse games, including a wide range of Atari games.

This study derives new, tight bounds for causal effects under missing data and measurement errors in outcomes. By leveraging these bounds, we develop non-parametric and computationally efficient estimators capable of handling high-dimensional data with possible non-substantially missing information. Our approach relies on the back-door adjustment formula and provides explicit estimator variance, enabling optimal weighting estimation through OLS. We validate the efficacy of these estimators through simulations and apply them to analyze gene expression data, yielding more accurate causal inferences.

This study focuses on developing efficient predictive methods to identify stealthy cyber attacks on systems, where direct detection is not possible due to limitations in computational resources and sensor data. Traditional approaches rely on storing extensive historical data, which is impractical for long-term monitoring. Instead, we propose an online prediction technique that leverages previous predictions to detect attacks in real-time. By employing a state-space model, we propose two online prediction methods: a recursive approach and a sliding window method. The recursive approach, with lower computational requirements, involves a single matrix inversion, while the sliding window method requires multiple inversions. Furthermore, we analyze the computational complexity of our methods and demonstrate their effectiveness through simulations.

A groundbreaking paper introduces an innovative graph-based model capable of summarizing text in languages Indian speakers use, all without requiring annotated data for training. The model capitalizes on the inherent structure of the text and leverages learned representations to produce coherent summaries. The implementation of the model is publicly accessible via the GitHub repository 'GAE-ISumm'.

We establish the definition and certain properties of S-rings of Krull type, in addition to exploring the relationship between S-ring factor automorphisms and abelian normal factors of particular types. This investigation leads to demonstrating that S-rings of finite Krull type exist.

Recent studies have identified a pattern of mass loss in five nearby stars, where the lost mass is likely expelled into space. The five stars in question are $\tau$ Ceti, $\sigma$ Oct, HD 12896, Gliese 876, and Gliese 817. The mass lost by these stars could be the result of interactions with their companion objects. To investigate this, researchers analyzed the companion objects' properties using available data and theoretical models. The analysis revealed that for $\tau$ Ceti, a Jupiter-like planet at a distance of 20-30 AU could explain the mass loss. The companion of $\sigma$ Oct is likely a brown dwarf with a mass of around 0.05 solar masses at a distance of 100 AU. The companion of HD 12896 could be a brown dwarf with a mass of around 0.06 solar masses at a distance of 10 AU. The mass loss of Gliese 876 and Gliese 817 can be explained by interactions with their planetary companions. The research suggests that the mass loss of these stars is likely due to interactions with their companion objects, rather than the ejection of material into space.

Deep learning models, particularly those like Variational Autoencoders, are often trained using maximum likelihood methods, which can be inefficient in certain situations. In this paper, we introduce a new, regularized Variational Autoencoder model based on a Bayesian framework, replacing the traditional likelihood with a least square loss function. This modification enhances the network's ability to reconstruct data and also provides insights into data generation. Our model's success is demonstrated through experiments on several datasets, including MNIST, CIFAR10, and CelebA.

As the number of IoT devices continues to rise, security and monitoring become increasingly vital concerns. The current IoT security and monitoring systems have several limitations, including high energy consumption, low accuracy, and low availability of private information. To address these issues, we propose a private blockchain-based smart home monitoring system that utilizes a lightweight localization technique and a smart contract to track IoT devices' location, energy consumption, and other private data. The smart contract enables users to access this private data with permission, while the localization method has been shown to require only 1.5% more energy than the devices' normal operation, thus ensuring a low energy consumption for the monitoring system.

A novel deep learning-based method for quantizing bit sequences, known as L-values, in various modulations is presented. By leveraging deep learning, the dependency between L-values is exploited to generate the subsequent sequence, thereby reducing quantization noise and enhancing the performance of the communication system. A single convolutional neural network is used to generate the next L-value based on the current sequence, thereby establishing a generative model. To facilitate the quantization process, the convolutional neural network is combined with a variational autoencoder, which learns the probability distribution of the modulation scheme. As a result, the proposed method achieves superior performance over traditional methods, particularly in the case of 64-QAM and other modulations.

We have developed parameterized algorithms for determining and drawing directed graphs in a valid upward planar layout based on specific characteristics. For the case of 3-outerplanar graphs, we've created an algorithm with a runtime of O(* + 2^n), allowing for either the creation of a valid layout or determination of its nonexistence. Additionally, we've developed a parameterized algorithm for testing and drawing 1-vertex series-parallel graphs with a runtime of O(* m^2 log m).

Crowdsourced data, despite its potential for large-scale use, often suffers from inaccuracies due to human error. To address this issue, conventional noise-removal techniques have been employed, but they typically require either a large number of responses per item or a prior understanding of correct responses. In this paper, an innovative approach utilizing ensemble modeling is presented to mitigate data inaccuracies in crowdsourced datasets. This method relies on an "human softmax" distribution, which captures the variability in crowd responses and can be applied to datasets with limited information. Ensemble modeling further enhances the approach by combining predictions from multiple models to improve overall accuracy.

For semiflows with uniformly or nonuniformly expanding dynamics, which exhibit exponential decay in correlations, we can prove the exponential decay in the H\"older norm of the transfer operators acting on smooth observables.

A particular type of data matrix, known as a covering array with index λ and parameters m × n, is designed such that every possible combination of its m rows includes all n symbols in every possible combination of its columns. The goal of this paper is to identify the structural properties of the minimum-size matrices of this type for a limited set of m and s values. The authors also provide a general method for constructing a matrix of this type with the minimum size for a given set of symbols, and they verify this method for certain specific cases.

We investigate the decidability of determining the optimal winning probability in two-player nonlocal games involving states of the form $\omega^{\otimes n}=(\omega^{(d)}\otimes\omega^{(d)})^{\otimes n}$, where $\omega$ is the maximally entangled state. This specific problem is a restricted form of the quantum nonlocal game decision problem, which was previously identified as an open question. The main achievement in our study is the demonstration that for any given nonlocal game and a desired level of precision, the optimal winning probability can be computed by a Turing machine. This outcome is a direct consequence of a more general theorem, showing that nonlocal games with a bounded number of inputs and any $d$-dimensional state $\rho$ have a computationally determined optimal winning probability.

This study aims to assess the effectiveness of a Guided Genetic Algorithm employed in crash reproduction, utilizing the SimCity 4 simulation software. By analyzing the algorithm's performance in this specific program, the results can inform the development of Guided Genetic Algorithms for other applications. This work involves replicating the original study's findings with reduced computational resources, specifically using a smaller subset of the program's file system and limited processing power.

By utilizing scanning SQUID microscopy, we have directly observed the intricate dynamics of vortex lattices in Bi$_2$Sr$_2$CaCu$_2$$\textrm{O}_{8+\delta}$ thin films under varying magnetic and temperature conditions. Our research reveals a previously unexplored region of vortex lattice transitions, specifically within the narrow temperature range of the sample, where an intermediate phase emerges between the expected square and triangular lattices. This intermediate phase exhibits characteristics of a gradual evolution from a square lattice at higher temperatures to a triangular lattice at lower temperatures, with the coexistence of square and diagonal vortex patterns observed in the intermediate phase. Our results provide significant insight into the complex behavior of high-temperature superconductors and shed light on the elusive nature of vortex lattice transitions within these materials.

Researchers have used direct photon measurements to determine the influence of momentum conservation on the elliptic flow ($v_2$) in heavy-ion collisions at top LHC energies. By applying a kinetic theory model that incorporates quark and gluon interactions, they found that momentum-conserving effects reduce photon $v_2$ by approximately 30%, significantly impacting its magnitude. This connection between photon $v_2$ and the properties of quark-gluon plasma allows for a non-perturbative determination of its viscosity-to-entropy density ratio.

We examine the behavior of magnetic systems with triangular and kagome structures, considering the effects of uniaxial anisotropy within the J_1-J_2 Heisenberg model. Our analysis focuses on the regimes where J_1 and J_2 dominate, and we employ mean field theory to investigate the phase diagrams. This model accurately predicts the magnetic order in both the dominant J_1 regime and the dominant J_2 regime, and our findings align with Monte Carlo simulations and previous studies. Moreover, our phase diagram exhibits consistency with experimental observations in materials such as kagome metals and Kondo systems, as well as the magnetic structure of kagome antiferromagnet YbMgSn.

Large-scale data analysis often involves analyzing multiple correlated outcomes, and in such cases, methods like the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure can control false discovery rates but may lack power when dealing with dependent data. To address this, a new class of dependent multiple testing procedures has been developed, and under certain conditions, they can control false discovery rates. However, these methods do not directly address the practical question of identifying which specific variables are affected by a treatment. To fill this gap, dependent data methods have been adapted to pinpoint the variables most significantly impacted by the treatment, and under certain conditions, the variables identified using these methods are likely to be the ones most significantly impacted by the treatment, and the number of correctly identified variables using these methods is likely to be greater than or equal to the number of variables identified using a standard procedure like the Benjamini-Hochberg method. To further test the effectiveness of these methods, additional data analysis has been performed using both simulated and actual data, and the results show that these methods can identify significant treatment effects more accurately and efficiently than the standard procedure.

The foundational aspects of cosmological inflation are explored. The derivation of equations governing the inflaton field, an introduction to slow-roll parameters, and a description of how inflationary perturbations are established, are key components. The advantages of the inflationary model in explaining the characteristics of the universe are also considered.

The CDF II collaboration's $W$ boson mass measurement deviates from the Standard Model prediction by $7.0\,\sigma$.  We investigate whether this anomalous $W$ mass and a discrepancy in the muon magnetic dipole moment can be explained by a type-X two Higgs doublet model. In our analysis, the $W$ mass and magnetic dipole moment anomalies can be jointly addressed by a type-X two Higgs doublet model featuring a light scalar around 125 GeV, along with an additional scalar mass of either 100 GeV or 1 TeV under constraints from experimental data.

Software developers often struggle with finding the correct concept when searching for it, due to uncertainties in their search queries. This issue can be mitigated by QUICKAR, an automated query reformulation system that utilizes crowd-sourced knowledge to suggest more effective searches. By analyzing crowd-sourced data, such as JSource, QUICKAR generates ranked concept recommendations that assist developers in locating the desired code elements.

Adaptation in conversational speech, known as entrainment, is a well-documented phenomenon where speakers adjust their utterances to align with their conversation partners. Researchers have long been interested in measuring the degree of entrainment, but existing metrics are often based on subjective assessments, which can be unreliable. In this study, we explore the potential of using deep neural networks to discover and quantify objective patterns of entrainment in conversational speech, specifically focusing on the alignment of acoustic features and lexical content. Our research demonstrates that deep learning models can effectively identify and capture meaningful patterns of entrainment, which may have practical applications in the development of more natural and adaptive conversational agents.

We have developed an open-source suite of web-based tools for the analysis and visualization of multi-wavelength astronomical data, including radio continuum, sub-millimeter, and spectral data. The tools, which are now version 2, offer significant enhancements over the original release, incorporating new capabilities such as the calculation and visualization of radio continuum spectra, sub-millimeter maps, and custom-defined spectral data. The tools have been designed to accommodate a wide range of use cases, from the analysis of individual astronomical objects to the comparative study of multiple sources. The tools' source code is hosted on GitHub, and their deployment on various cloud platforms is also documented.

Identifying the precise start and end of actions within unlabeled videos is a complex task. Traditional methods rely heavily on hand-crafted features or annotated data, which is time-consuming and costly to obtain. A new approach, utilizing self-supervised learning techniques, has shown promise in tackling this challenge without requiring extensive annotations. A key issue in this area is that existing self-supervised methods often overlook the critical action parsing phase, which is essential for pinpointing the exact action boundaries. A novel method, called SSCAP, has been developed to address this limitation by combining self-supervised learning with action parsing. SSCAP's unique two-way approach allows it to leverage both video and parsed action information to produce a precise action parsing without requiring any annotations. Experimental results demonstrate that SSCAP achieves superior performance compared to other state-of-the-art methods in both video understanding and action parsing tasks.

The existence of the $P_{cs}(4459)$ and $P_{cs}(4358)$ charmed-strange states has been confirmed by the LHCb collaboration. The goal of this research is to understand the internal structure of these states and other related states such as the $P_{cs}(4338)$, $P_{cs}(4463)$, $P_{cs}(4570)$, and $P_{sc}(4696)$ states. The study utilizes the current algebra approach to calculate the production rates of these states in various reactions, including the $e^+e^-$, $\gamma p$, and $\bar{p} p$ processes. The results of this research suggest that the observed states are likely composed of a compact five-quark configuration. The study also investigates the properties of the $P_{cs}(4338)$ state and its potential interactions with other states. The production of the $P_{cs}(4338)$ state is primarily through the $e^+e^-$ and $\gamma p$ reactions, while its decays into $J/\psi \Sigma$ and $\Lambda_c \bar{D}$ channels are predicted to be significant. The study also predicts the production rates of the $P_{cs}(4459)$ and $P_{cs}(4358)$ states in various reactions, including the $\gamma p$,

In computer science education, formative feedback is a crucial component for student growth.  Current practices often involve providing explanations for student errors, yet an alternative approach called Informed Inquiry (II) has been gaining attention.  This method involves students identifying their mistakes and offering solutions, which can be more effective than traditional feedback.  We conducted a comprehensive study to evaluate the efficacy of II compared to conventional detailed feedback in a computer science education setting.  By implementing both methods in an introductory software testing course, we were able to assess their effectiveness in improving student performance.  Our findings revealed that II outperformed traditional feedback in helping students grasp the course material and excel in testing activities.  Moreover, students who received the traditional feedback reported a greater desire for additional support.  These results suggest that educators should consider adopting the II method to enhance student learning and growth.

Domain adaptation is a machine learning technique that enables knowledge transfer from a source domain to a different target domain. Traditional approaches require access to labeled source domain data, but this is often impractical. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel source-free domain adaptation method called Semi-Supervised Hypothesis Transfer (SHT). Slever utilizes the hypothesis that the target domain data is likely to be labeled in large quantities. Specifically, SHT employs two semi-supervised learning techniques - Co-Training and Contrastive Learning - to improve the model's ability to make accurate predictions. Our SHT method outperforms state-of-the-art methods in several benchmark tasks, including image classification and cross-domain sentiment analysis.

A novel nuclear propulsion system, characterized by a gas core reactor, is proposed for interplanetary travel. This design utilizes a contained plasma mixture of fissile material and helium, enabling the plasma to float within a magnetic field due to its density being lower than the surrounding structure. The unique characteristics of this design allow for higher energy output and greater thermal efficiency compared to traditional solid fuel systems. By leveraging computational fluid dynamics simulations, this research evaluates the feasibility of this concept, demonstrating that it can achieve substantial power generation and superior thrust capabilities.

Neural networks have become a prominent choice for analyzing large volumes of data in particle physics, particularly for identifying complex patterns. However, their "black box" nature makes it difficult to pinpoint the specific input features influencing their predictions. A novel approach, known as a domain-informed neural network, has been developed to address this limitation by integrating crucial physical constraints into the analysis. This method has been successfully applied to localize interactions within large liquid argon detectors, and experiments have shown that it can accurately capture the relevant characteristics of the data, thereby outperforming traditional detection methods in identifying the detectors' signals.

The study of substellar exoplanet atmospheres relies heavily on the analysis of spectral absorption, which heavily depends on the availability of accurate molecular absorption cross-sections. Unfortunately, a comprehensive and up-to-date database of these cross-sections is currently lacking. To address this gap, a new database called EXOPLINES has been developed, which provides a comprehensive collection of molecular absorption cross-sections for 18 key molecules, including H2O, CH4, CO, CO2, and others, all of which are essential for understanding the atmospheres of substellar exoplanets. The database, designed to be easily accessible and compatible with various analysis tools, has been integrated into popular tools such as TauREx 3 and has been optimized for specific applications, including the analysis of data from the James Webb Space Telescope.

This study investigates the theoretical basis of grounding in Answer Set Programming, a process that involves limiting the scope of the program to finite subsets of Herbrand domains and function Herbrand universes. We examine two established grounding methods, focusing on their fundamental properties and the novel abstract grounding operator proposed in [2]. The findings of this investigation have potential applications for the development of infinite ASP programs and the analysis of their behavior in infinite contexts.

We have developed a resource theory applicable to all multipartite quantum states and found that its resource theory is equivalent to the entanglement promotion task. We have proven that a single, comprehensive monotone governs this theory, and this monotone is both necessary and sufficient to determine the relationships between states, including when one state can be transformed into another using only completely positive and trace-preserving maps. We have derived a first law governing the change in this monotone under any multipartite quantum operations, and we have shown that this theory is equivalent to several well-known resource theories, including those of negativity, randomness, nonlocality, Bell nonlocality, hyperdeviating channels, and magic states.

To assess information content, we consider a decision maker with limited knowledge about a random variable's distribution. Our approach focuses on the minimal information required for specific purposes, such as a decision maker's optimal choice or prediction. We introduce a new method to measure this information, the information functional, which remains consistent across different utility functions and remains unchanged when relevant data is added. We examine the properties of this information measure, such as its relationship with the mean, median, higher moments, variability, and higher-order utility theory.

We investigate the interdependence of multiple time series with complex statistical properties, focusing on linear relationships and innovations. An estimated covariance matrix of the series is proposed, which can be interpreted as the conditional expectation of the covariance matrix of one series given another, even when the series are not stationary. We prove the consistency of the proposed estimator under various heavy-tailed distributions and demonstrate its practical value by applying it to real-world scenarios, including analyzing the behavior of multiple stocks during financial crises.

A novel set of quantum low-density parity-check codes is introduced, which was first proposed in [KW18]. These codes, which are constructed from collision graphs, have specific properties regarding their check and variable nodes' degrees, denoted as R and D respectively. What makes these codes particularly noteworthy is their ability to be decoded efficiently in O(n log n) or even O(n) time. Furthermore, research in [KW18] demonstrated that these codes possess good distance and rate characteristics. In this paper, we present a significant advancement by developing an implementation of the belief propagation decoder capable of achieving constant factor distance and rate performance, specifically an implementation with O(n) time complexity.

Determining whether a graph has a distance-$r$ dominating set is an NP-complete problem for every $r \geq 1$. In this paper, we investigate whether such a problem can be solved efficiently in a distributed environment. Specifically, we focus on two types of graphs: those with high girth and those with a specific sparsity constraint. By adapting a known result, we demonstrate that for any fixed $r$, finding a distance-$1$ dominating set can be solved in a specific number of steps for graphs with sufficiently large cycles. However, this efficient result cannot be achieved in all cases, as we show that the problem remains complex even in a specific type of graph structure. Moreover, we establish a lower bound on the minimum number of steps required to solve the distance-$r$ dominating set problem in a specific type of graph structure.

This research investigates the impact of disorder on the correlation between bulk and boundaries in topological insulators of higher order. Specifically, we explore how disorder affects the 1D corner states and 2D hinge states within 3D insulators of higher topological nature. To achieve this, we utilize the disordered Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model and apply the winding number to calculate bulk topological invariants in the presence of disorder. Our results demonstrate that monotonically increasing disorder can cause the topological invariants to transition from non-zero to zero values. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between bulk topological invariants and corner/hinge states under varying levels of disorder. Our findings suggest that corner states remain stable against disorder up to a certain threshold, while hinge states exhibit different disorder tolerance depending on their orientation.

Recent searches for supersymmetry at the CMS have not yet provided any conclusive evidence for a particular model. In response, the CMS has been carrying out model-independent supersymmetry searches, which are not tied to a particular theoretical framework. These searches have been conducted across a wide range of masses and supersymmetry scenarios, with the results presented in this context, with the focus on dilepton final states.

Novel view synthesis using light field representation offers a straightforward and efficient approach to rendering scenes from multiple viewpoints, albeit limited to small baseline shifts. Conversely, deep learning-based methods excel in globally consistent novel view synthesis but often struggle with generalizability and computational efficiency. This paper introduces a novel technique that combines the strengths of both methods by integrating light field geometry with neural rendering. The proposed framework, Light Field Neural Rendering, leverages neural rendering to bridge the gap between multiple light field captures, thereby overcoming the LFR limit. The framework's components, Light Field Inpainting and Light Field Fusion, handle missing view data, while the Generalized Light Field module enables view extrapolation. The research demonstrates the efficacy of the framework in various applications, including dense view synthesis, super-resolution, and novel view extension.

Observations conducted at the SOAR telescope in 2020 yielded 104 successful datasets for speckle interferometry, out of a total of 126 attempted, utilizing a 2.5-meter aperture. The majority of these successful datasets, comprising 81, focused on observing binary and multiple star systems, while the remaining 23 targeted single stars, primarily to study atmospheric distortion and turbulence. The observed targets spanned a spectral range from 300 to 880 nanometers, with 170 high-resolution speckle images captured at a wavelength of 606 nanometers, allowing the detection of binary systems down to a separation of 1.5 milliarcseconds, with 12 new binary systems identified. The study of binary and multiple star systems revealed 8 new orbital parameters, with 5 previously unknown companions discovered. The speckle imaging of single stars facilitated the measurement of full-width half-maxima values for 88 stars, with 17 previously unmeasured, and provided the full-width half-maxima measurement for HD 127921 at 0.51 ± 0.02 milliarcseconds. The study also measured the full-width half-maxima of HD 189733A at two different wavelengths, yielding values of 0.49 ± 0.02 milliarcseconds at 550 nanometers and

We are investigating chiral celestial algebras within the framework of celestial holography, discovering that the 3-point kinematic algebra is not complete and we suggest an enhanced version. This revised algebra is designed to be closed under the star product and has a dual counterpart in conformal field theory, which we propose as a remedy. We further explore potential connections between this improved algebra and other areas of study, including the kinematic algebra of N=4 super Yang-Mills theory, the operator algebra of a 2D CFT with central charge c=1, and the integrable properties of the latter.

A widely accepted theory suggests that solar shocks are formed by jets emanating from active regions, yet direct evidence for piston shock formation by jets in the low corona has been scarce. This research presents the discovery of a piston shock in the low solar corona, formed by a jet emanating from a relatively quiet area of the Sun. The analysis of multi-frequency images and Doppler shift maps reveals a piston shock in the low corona, accompanied by an X-ray shock wave detected by the RHESSI satellite. The observed piston shock exhibits characteristics consistent with those predicted by the fast magnetosonic shock model, including shock angle, shock width, and post-shock jet velocity. The detection of this piston shock at close proximity to the Sun provides crucial insights into the formation of shocks in the solar corona and may also be a common phenomenon.

A comprehensive likelihood analysis is performed on the general two Higgs doublet model, taking into account the Standard Model's particle spectrum and interaction strengths. This analysis considers all available experimental data from the LHCb and ATLAS experiments, as well as BaBar and Belle studies on $B\to DK$ decays, and the results are compared with the LHC's findings on di-Higgs production. Furthermore, the model's predictions are evaluated in relation to the muon's anomalous magnetic moment and the Higgs self-coupling. This research provides an in-depth understanding of the model's parameter space and its compatibility with the Standard Model's parameters.

This work introduces a groundbreaking method for simulating the dynamic behavior of random vortex systems in a two-dimensional space. By applying stochastic principles, we develop a functional stochastic differential equation that accurately captures the movement of random vortex systems. To make this approach computationally feasible, we develop a stochastic finite difference method, which we then use to run simulations. Through numerical experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this method by comparing its results to the actual solutions. Furthermore, we assess the accuracy of the proposed approach in terms of both discrete values and trajectory approximations.

The phenomenon of boson sampling relies on fundamental quantum principles and has been applied in various quantum information tasks. However, its application has not extensively explored the concept of entanglement. Our study examines the generation and measurement of entanglement within the full state vector of boson sampling, using two distinct approaches: the Slater rank method for fermionic systems and an entropy-based method for general quantum systems. The results demonstrate that the Slater rank method is suitable for boson sampling, and numerical simulations reveal that the Slater rank of the resulting state increases with the number of photons, indicating a state of partial entanglement. Furthermore, experiments utilizing spontaneous parametric down-conversion have successfully measured the entanglement produced in boson sampling, and our data show that the experimentally observed entanglement aligns with our theoretical predictions.

Temporal sequence data analysis in life science research is a significant challenge due to the diversity of measurements and their associated complexities.
To address this issue, a new, unsupervised method for identifying meaningful temporal patterns in various life science measurements is presented.
A key aspect of this method involves using a supervised learning approach based on dynamic time warping to establish a connection between the discovered patterns and relevant biological or medical knowledge.
A prototype system demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach is exemplified through its application to analyzing calcium signals from individual brain cells.

Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have been extensively studied for their ability to encode time-invariant beliefs in partially observable tasks. However, the specific mechanisms by which RNNs derive these beliefs from past experiences remain unclear. This research demonstrates that RNN beliefs can be understood as a combination of two key factors: an internal belief state, which is determined through Bayesian integration, and the RNN's hidden state that captures past states. By employing variational inference, we can train RNNs to approximate the true belief state and reveal how their hidden states track agent beliefs over time. This discovery highlights the significance of historical state representations learned by RNNs in their internal models.

In video action detection, identifying actions within specific timeframes proves challenging, particularly when actions are not explicitly marked. This paper introduces an innovative weakly-supervised approach, leveraging only video clip titles as training data. Our proposed method, called Graph Convolutional Network (GCN), utilizes a graph model to capture action context, thereby enhancing performance. Specifically, GCN uses a binary graph to represent spatio-temporal relationships, and a two-stage model is developed to efficiently utilize this information. The first stage employs a CNN to generate initial predictions, while the second stage refines these using the GCN-based binary graph to capture long-range dependencies. Our experimental results on MSVD and Kinetics datasets demonstrate GCN's superiority over state-of-the-art weakly-supervised and supervised methods.

The Image Similarity Challenge 2021 (ISC21) is a benchmark competition that
evaluates and compares image retrieval models using the latest ImageNet dataset.
This paper presents the paper selection process, various categories, results from
the main competition, outcomes of the special events, and the paper selection
process for the upcoming ISC22.

This work explores the stability of diffusion processes across diverse environments, encompassing uniform and highly varied landscapes. Our focus lies in understanding the evolution of a diffusion process over extended periods, subjected to external disturbances. Specifically, we investigate the long-term behavior of the solution to a time-dependent parabolic partial differential equation, encompassing a range of boundary conditions. We examine the metastability of solutions in scenarios where the diffusion coefficient approaches zero at specific spatial points, as well as the effects of rapidly oscillating diffusion coefficients on solution behavior.

The impact of extremely strong magnetic fields on nuclear matter properties is explored through the lens of finite nuclear systems. Utilizing the (ρ,σ) mean field equation of state derived from the local density approximation variant of the Coulomb hole correlation method with the $^{16}$O potential, the effects of various magnetic field strengths on the emergence of spin-polarized matter are examined. Our results reveal that intense magnetic fields cause a significant increase in the emergence density of spin-polarized matter, whereas magnetic fields have relatively minimal influence on the emergence of isospin-polarized matter.

Protecting user privacy is a top priority in distributed machine learning applications. This study proposes an innovative approach that reconciles the principles of differential privacy and secure communication in federated learning networks. The method, known as DP-REC, integrates dynamic differential privacy and efficient communication strategies to enhance the overall performance of FL training. By incorporating noise reduction techniques and communication optimizations, DP-REC achieves a balance between data confidentiality and model effectiveness. Experimental results validate the efficacy of DP-REC, showcasing its ability to surpass existing DP methods in both efficiency and performance.

A comprehensive far-ultraviolet survey of the Taurus-Perseus-Auriga star-forming complex has been conducted, focusing on the young stars within these areas.  The investigation involved the use of the FUSE telescope to obtain the first direct observations in the 90-118 nm wavelength range.  The results indicate that the young stars in the regions emit significant amounts of far-ultraviolet radiation, with the energy output of the source exceeding 10^32 erg/s.  The emission spectrum is characterized by a strong continuum and prominent interstellar absorption lines, with the optical depth of the absorption decreasing with increasing wavelength.  The interstellar material exhibits a high column density and a high abundance of certain elements, with the A0V star HD 36916 located in the Auriga region.  The observations also revealed the presence of a blue continuum component in the emission spectrum, with the energy output of the source exceeding 10^32 erg/s.
