The origin of Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) remains a major unsolved problem in astrophysics. Observations of FRBs in the optical spectrum could provide crucial insights into their origins. We conducted a search for optical emission from the sub-arcsecond localized FRBs identified by the CHIME/FRB project. Our search used the Dark Energy Camera to capture deep images of the FRBs' positions at the time of the bursts. No significant optical emission was detected, leading to the most stringent limits on the optical-to-radio energy ratio for FRBs. Our findings indicate that any optical emission associated with FRBs must be extremely faint, with an upper limit of $10^{-10}$ to $10^{-11}$ times the burst's radio energy. Our results also suggest that the optical emission associated with FRBs is unlikely to be linked to the optical supernovae associated with repeating FRB sources. Our findings have implications for models of FRB origins, particularly those involving the magnetar as the source of the bursts.

The development of high-power laser systems is crucial for applications such as directed energy and ultrashort pulse generation. Achieving high energy and short pulse duration requires complex laser systems, which can be designed using a combination of machine learning and nonlinear dynamics. This study utilizes a deep neural network to model the behavior of active and passive laser components, allowing for the simulation of their behavior under various conditions. This model is then used to optimize the performance of each component, taking into account the constraints of the system. This approach has been successfully applied to optimize a Yb:YAG laser amplifier, resulting in an increase in output energy and pulse duration. Furthermore, this study demonstrates the potential of using machine learning to reverse-engineer unknown laser systems, by training a neural network to model the behavior of a Raman amplifier and using it to infer its characteristics from experimental data. This research has significant implications for the development of high-power laser systems, as it provides a new approach to optimizing and reverse-engineering these complex systems.

Recent breakthroughs in language modeling have led to the creation of highly capable text-generating models. However, it's still unclear how these models can be guided to process visual information. Our research proposes a new method called VPL that integrates a series of carefully designed visual controls into the text generation process. These control tokens allow a model to process and integrate visual information from an image, even when it's not explicitly requested. Through a series of experiments, we demonstrate VPL's effectiveness in addressing various challenges, such as detecting and correcting visual hallucinations, and leveraging visual cues to improve performance on complex tasks like visual reasoning and multi-image understanding.

We introduce an innovative transaction protocol, Delegated RingCT, which enhances the原有的 RingCT protocol by enabling swifter anonymous transactions. Our solution, Delegated RingCT, is comprised of two components: a Delegator that facilitates rapid verification of a fraction of a transaction's proof, and a Delegator-aided RingCT that enables faster transactions while maintaining ringCT's level of anonymity. Our Delegated RingCT protocol outperforms the coinjoin protocol in terms of transaction speed, and demonstrates comparable anonymity to both ringCT and coinjoin. Our results indicate that Delegated RingCT offers a viable option for users seeking to transact quickly without sacrificing anonymity.

Future high-energy colliders, operating at extremely high luminosity levels, will be heavily influenced by the horizontal beta function at their interaction points. Optimizing this parameter, along with understanding beam diagnostics, is crucial for maximizing luminosity. As a result, new types of diagnostics, employing specialized detectors, will be developed to measure key parameters at full luminosity. These measurements, involving both transverse and longitudinal beam characteristics, will be carried out in three dimensions to provide an in-depth understanding of beam behavior under saturated beam-beam effects.

The widespread adoption of data-driven modeling in science and engineering is driven by the promise of achieving significant performance enhancements. However, the current approach of developing models in isolation is often plagued by limitations such as subpar performance, extended development timelines, and excessive computational requirements. To address these challenges, we introduce a cooperative data-driven modeling framework that leverages collective problem-solving capabilities. By combining the strengths of various data-driven models, our framework can substantially boost prediction accuracy and accelerate development and deployment times. Moreover, our approach optimizes resource utilization by enabling the parallel deployment of models on different computing resources. The efficacy of this innovative framework is demonstrated through a case study involving the prediction of turbulent flows in complex internal systems.

This research investigates the decay of the $\Upsilon(10753)$ into a $\Upsilon(nS)$ and a $\pi\pi$ pair, with $n$ being 2 or 3. It focuses on the role of hadronic loops in mediating this process and uses this to study the nature of the newly discovered $\Upsilon(10753)$, specifically whether it is a hadronic molecule made up of $\Upsilon(10526)$ and $\pi\pi$. The study finds that loop contributions to certain decay processes involving $\pi\pi$ are substantial and can significantly impact their overall decay rates. The decay of the $\Upsilon(10753)$ into $\Upsilon(2S)\pi\pi$ is predicted to occur at a rate of $1.15\%$, while the $\Upsilon(10753)$'s decay into $\Upsilon(3S)\pi\pi$ is estimated at $0.19\%$.

This paper presents a novel optimization approach called AskewSGD, which is designed to efficiently train quantized neural networks. Traditional quantization methods, such as rounding weights to integers, often compromise the accuracy of these networks. However, by constraining real-valued weights to specific intervals and training them using an SGD-based algorithm, we can achieve better quantization results. Our proposed method, AskewSGD, is an acceleration technique that further enhances the convergence rate of this process. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through experiments on image classification tasks, where it achieves improved accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods.

The versatility of soft robots in navigating complex environments has led to their application in a wide range of industries. Due to the inherent complexities of their dynamics, employing traditional control techniques is often insufficient. The development of model-based control methods, which integrate physical models to enhance performance, has been crucial in improving soft robots' capabilities. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of recent advancements in the model-based control of soft robots, focusing on state-of-the-art techniques and their applications to various soft robot designs. We also outline future research directions and key challenges to be addressed in this field.

This study examines the group J consisting of matrices $\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}$ with real values, which satisfy the equation $ab+cd=0$. We have found a way to complete the group J by adding elements that form a compact space C, resulting in the completion $\bar{J}=C+J$. We have also determined the structure of C and $\bar{J}$, which comprises multiple components, each comprising a compact element and two invariant manifolds derived from the original Jacobi equation.

Recent research has focused on using language models to verify facts by checking if a statement holds true given a corresponding table. To date, most methods rely on combining the outputs of individual cells, which can be problematic due to the varied structure of different table formats. To address this limitation, we introduce an innovative approach that involves breaking down complex tables into fundamental components, which not only simplifies the task but also enhances model performance across various datasets, including Cosmos and FEVER.

Deep learning models, specifically Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), have been extensively used for creating realistic images. However, they have limitations in generating images with specific content. To overcome these limitations, researchers have developed methods for controlling the images produced by the models. This paper presents an investigation into how different conditioning techniques affect the ability to generate desired images within the space of latent space in the case of GANs.

We introduce a novel algorithm for nested sampling that employs Metropolis-Hastings to explore the space of truncation indices under the posterior distribution. We develop and compare four distinct approaches to construct proposals within this framework. The analysis, carried out using synthetic data in two contexts - a simple parameter estimation task and a model selection problem involving the Excess Mean Mixture model - reveals that two of the proposed moves are consistently efficient. The excess mean mixture case also allows us to investigate the impact of hyperparameters on the performance of the nested sampling methods we examine.

This paper introduces distance labeling schemes for planar graphs with improved worst-case performance and novel fault-tolerant capabilities. Specifically, it provides a scheme with $O(\sqrt n)$ query time and $O(\log^2 n)$ label size for finding the shortest path between any two vertices, and $O(\log^2 n / \sqrt{\log \log n})$ for vertex deletion queries, with a limit of $O(\log^3 n)$ on vertex insertion query complexity. Furthermore, it achieves $O(\log^2 n)$ label size and $O(\log^2 n / \sqrt{\log \log n})$ vertex deletion query time, while allowing $O(\log^2 n)$ insertion query time and $O(n^{1/2+\epsilon})$ query time for any $\epsilon > 0$. These advancements build upon prior work by Demaine et al. and represent significant improvements in both efficiency and adaptability.

In the thermodynamic limit, we investigate the time-domain two-particle correlation functions of a Bose-Hubbard model subject to external driving and dissipation, with a particular focus on how these correlations are affected by the interplay of driving and dissipation. Our analysis reveals that when driving and dissipation are perfectly balanced, i.e., in steady state, two distinct types of correlations emerge: one that is long-range and another that is short-range. These findings are further validated through the use of numerical methods and matrix product state approximations. In addition, we explore the dynamical behavior of two-particle correlations following a sudden change in system parameters. In this context, we discover that a particular type of quench can lead to the emergence of long-range correlations even in systems that typically exhibit short-range interactions. In contrast, a particular type of quench can lead to the emergence of short-range correlations even in systems that typically exhibit long-range correlations. These findings are further validated through the use of numerical methods.

The solutions to divergence-form elliptic equations with added drift terms are analyzed, with a focus on their $L^p$ estimates for $p$ ranging between 1 and infinity. By establishing these estimates, we obtain $L^p$-theory for a class of second-order elliptic equations and a Lyapunov inequality for those with an $L^2$-gradient coefficient.

Deep neural networks have proven effective at identifying patterns within specific datasets but often fail when presented with new, unseen distributions. This limitation is particularly evident in the field of Out-of-Distribution (OOD) detection. A novel approach, OOD detection using Distributional Gaussian Processes (DGP), is introduced. OOD detection using DGP involves training a probabilistic model on labeled data to estimate its likelihood for both labeled and unlabeled data. This method is then applied to a classification task using the OOD detection layer as a loss function. OOD detection using DGP is capable of generalizing well in various scenarios, including domain shift and corruption noise. This method is also compatible with pre-trained models, such as ResNet-50, and can be used in conjunction with other training methods to achieve even better results.

In the realm of quantum many-body systems, the phenomenon of high-temperature behavior resulting from periodic driving, known as Floquet heating, typically leads to a state of thermal disorder. However, a unique type of heating mechanism, referred to as "cold" or "scar-like" heating, can give rise to stable patterns of quantum behavior. This study explores the potential for Bose condensation within a specific "cold" heating scenario, involving a one-dimensional lattice of bosonic particles driven by a periodic force and connected to a surrounding thermal environment. The combination of Floquet heating and spatial correlations resulting from scanning-tunneling-microscopy-like driving patterns enables the emergence of stable phases of quantum behavior, even in the presence of thermal disorder.

We provide a concrete proof for the Alexandrov maximum principle in the context of the Monge-Ampere equation, building upon prior work by Buser, Berman-Burger, and Zhang. This proof is formulated within the framework of generalized solutions as defined by Caffarelli, Nirenberg, and Song. Notably, our approach is distinct from previous methods and yields an improved estimate for the modulus of continuity of the Laplacian, specifically in the range of $log(1/u)$, which aligns with the optimal bound initially proposed by Han and Song.

Optical clocks, renowned for their exceptional precision, have revolutionized our perception of time. Historically, their reliability has been confined to fixed intervals. However, recent breakthroughs have enabled their use in dynamic environments. To harness their potential, a new level of confidence in their performance is required, especially when they are employed in non-recurring scenarios. This study presents a statistical framework to assess the reliability of optical clocks in such dynamic settings, leveraging data from the world's first all-optical timekeeping system developed at the Max Planck Institute of Quantum Optics. This framework can be universally applied to clocks operating at any frequency, including those based on microwave technology, and is particularly valuable for future optical timekeeping systems that will be deployed in diverse and unpredictable environments.

This research introduces an SDN-based framework that utilizes fog computing to manage real-time services with strict deadlines. The proposed solution involves a two-tier architecture with a global controller and a local fast controller. The local fast controller oversees fog nodes, preventing failures and ensuring real-time requirements are met. Meanwhile, the global controller oversees the data center, preventing node failures and minimizing energy consumption. A joint optimization problem is formulated to determine the optimal placement of fog nodes and their operating modes. A specialized algorithm is developed to solve this problem, yielding near-optimal results. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, with significant improvements in service delivery and energy efficiency.

We introduce 'gradient surgery', a novel diagnostic tool for evaluating the
contribution of individual terms in a composite loss function to the overall
training process. By applying this method to several established deep learning
models, we thoroughly examine its effectiveness on functions such as focal loss,
label smoothing, and multi-task objectives. Our experiments reveal that gradient
surgery can accurately assess the impact of individual loss components, and
further analysis suggests that key techniques like focal loss and label smoothing
primarily serve to mitigate the effects of class imbalance.

We developed the hyper-invariant MERA, a novel quantum circuit error correction code, which achieves a constant error correction rate, $\delta$, up to a critical threshold of $\p$ by employing a hierarchical structure of disclinations with exponentially increasing scales, $\lambda^k$. The code's rate is expressed as $\delta = \p - \p$ where $\lambda$ represents the power-law exponent. Leveraging the properties of the hyper-invariant MERA, we constructed a quantum system exhibiting long-range correlations, characterized by a power-law decay of $\alpha = 3$. This construction offers a clear understanding of the relationship between the area law and the holographic principle, and it also provides a clear criterion for the critical behavior of holographic models.

Our analysis of Gaia DR3 data has led to the identification of 1,019 population members within 1.5 kpc of the Galactic Center. This allowed us to detect 1,113 filament segments, comprising a total of 1,619 filament members. Building upon our previous findings, we now examine the spatial distribution of these filament members, revealing that their arrangement is consistent with a population with a Gaussian velocity field. Moreover, we observe a population structured into filaments with an average inter-filament spacing of approximately 1,000 parsecs. This spacing aligns with the predicted size of molecular clouds in a galactic bar and supports the theory that these filaments originated from cloud mergers in the Galactic Bar.

This research introduces a distributed method to optimize conservation voltage reduction (CVR) in interconnected distribution networks. The study considers integrated primary-secondary systems where integrated transformers (ITs) regulate secondary voltages. An iterative approach is proposed, where a central authority sets a target for total energy loss reduction and allocates this target among participating ITs. Each IT calculates its optimal transformer tap setting and shares this setting with the central authority, which then updates its reduction target based on the shared tap settings. The process continues until convergence is achieved. The proposed method is validated through simulations on the IEEE 34-bus test system, demonstrating its effectiveness in reducing energy loss through coordinated IT tap settings.

We investigate non-stochastic bandits and experts in a unique setting where feedback is delayed differently for each arm or expert, given only after taking an action, and we call this feedback arm-dependent delayed feedback. This scenario is more realistic than the previously studied settings with uniform delays, and it also has the drawback of introducing more complicated problems. We introduce two novel algorithms for this setting, one for the multi-armed bandit problem and another for the expert problem, and we demonstrate their effectiveness by proving non-asymptotic regret bounds for both. Furthermore, we show that it is impossible to eliminate regret entirely in this setting, and our algorithms are optimal up to a constant factor.

Text-based dialogue has been a longstanding challenge in Natural Language Processing (NLP), and current language models often struggle to produce natural, engaging responses. To address this, a novel framework called LEATHER has been developed to generate dialogue that mirrors authentic human interaction. LEATHER achieves this by learning the underlying structure of conversations, known as dialogue acts, and using it to create responses that are both coherent and contextually appropriate. By incorporating a neural network that learns dialogue acts and using them as a guide for text generation, LEATHER can generate highly human-like dialogue. Evaluation of LEATHER demonstrates its ability to produce strong, conversational responses, and human feedback reveals that it generates more lifelike interactions than alternative methods.

This article examines the quantum chromodynamics (QCD) thermodynamics from the perspective of lattice Monte Carlo simulations at non-zero temperatures and densities. A brief overview of lattice QCD is provided to establish the framework for the discussion. The article delves into the effects of a non-zero quark mass, temperature, and density, and also explores the role of the electromagnetic interaction within the context of lattice QCD simulations at non-zero temperatures and densities.

A key challenge in managing offshore wind farms lies in their unpredictable output, which is heavily influenced by their location. To address this issue, researchers have developed probabilistic models to forecast the probabilistic behavior of wind turbines, which can also be applied to other areas such as predicting the reliability of components and the energy they produce over time. In this study, the authors employed Gaussian processes to create probabilistic models for the loads experienced by a hypothetical offshore wind turbine situated in a specified area, which was subjected to varying environmental conditions. These models were applied to the structural load of the turbine's tower, which was analyzed using a specific simulation method. The results showed that the developed models accurately captured the statistical behavior of the simulated data, which was further validated through confidence intervals. Additionally, the researchers observed that the developed models accurately predicted extreme values, which was crucial for assessing the risk of component failure.

This research investigates the application of Twitter as a tool for gathering and analyzing public sentiment surrounding the 30 June 2018 Izmir earthquake in Turkey. The study focuses on real-time public reaction data collected from Twitter following the earthquake, analyzing tweets based on their temporal and spatial characteristics. By employing an automated approach, the study extracts and categorizes tweet content into positive, negative, or neutral sentiment groups, and maps the geographical spread of these sentiments. By correlating sentiment analysis results with actual casualty figures, the study demonstrates the utility of Twitter data in understanding public response to natural disasters.

A group G is defined as having the $R_\infty$ property if, for every isomorphic involution $\phi$ in G, fixing the center of its $\phi$-twisted Alexander module's group, the rank of this center is infinite. This study expands upon prior findings by proving that certain generalized Baumslag-Solitar groups, specifically their nilpotent quotients, exhibit the $R_\infty$ property.

A new method is developed to analyze time-sensitive data by using an optimal basis set that outlines a system's evolution. This approach, based on a fundamental theorem of matrix analysis, provides the most efficient framework for describing changes over time. By applying a forward-optimization technique within this framework, the method is able to accurately model data even in the presence of significant noise. When tested with simulated data from a laser-driven process, the method successfully recovers time-resolved information with high precision, outperforming other analysis techniques. This approach has the potential to greatly advance time-resolved spectroscopy and pump-probe experiments.

Naturalistic Driving Study (NDS) data is crucial for developing autonomous vehicles and understanding human driving behavior. However, labeling this data is a complex task due to the vast variety of driving scenarios. This paper presents a dataset featuring a diverse range of scenarios, including highway driving, city environments, and parking, derived from the Naturalistic Driving Study-2. We introduce a novel deep learning-based method for automatically detecting NDS data using object detectors and temporal segmentations. The approach is evaluated against human annotations, demonstrating high accuracy in object detection and temporal segmentation.

This study explores the concept of reflected entropy in the context of boundary and
relevance entropy in the context of boundary conformal field theory. We examine
its behavior in the bulk and boundary of BCFT and TCFT under the influence of
repulsive and attractive boundary conditions. We derive a dual representation
of the reflected entropy in the context of the bulk/boundary OPE in the Lorentzian
limit. This dual representation enables us to derive a set of inequalities
governing the behavior of the reflected entropy. Additionally, this work
investigates the behavior of the reflected entropy in the boundary of the Ope
of the bulk and boundary Ope.

A revolutionary reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) is being extensively researched to optimize wireless communication systems. In our study, we propose a novel, end-to-end RIS-assisted orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) system that incorporates an enhanced extreme learning machine (e-ELM) channel estimation technique. This integrated approach addresses hardware limitations and mitigates the effects of noise within the channel. By employing a two-stage learning process, the e-ELM channel estimator achieves superior performance, surpassing conventional estimators. Furthermore, the proposed e-ELM RIS beamforming scheme demonstrates exceptional performance in terms of sum rate and robustness under resource constraints.

We have derived a single energy measurement based theorem for quantum systems, which is an extension of the integral fluctuation theorem observed in the measurement process. This type of energy measurement does not follow the standard projective measurement method. Instead, we use a generalized measurement approach and demonstrate that the energy measurement outcome is defined by the change in the eigenvalue of a Hamiltonian that matches the state's eigenstate. Furthermore, we investigate the characteristics of energy measurements in the context of two types of Hamiltonians: one that remains constant and one that varies with time.

We are examining the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. Firstly, we establish the conditions under which nearly G2-manifolds can be approximated by a real analytic metric from a smooth one. Next, we derive a linearized operator for the deformation of a G2-instanton and establish the existence and uniqueness of its solution under specific conditions. This is achieved through the application of the inverse function theorem, which in turn allows us to investigate the relationship between nearly G2-Einstein G2-instantons and instantons on seven-dimensional Heeger manifolds.

As the COVID-19 pandemic continues to spread globally, countries are adopting various strategies to contain the virus, including widespread use of contact tracing apps. These apps aim to identify and alert individuals who may have been exposed to the virus, but concerns have been raised about their ability to protect user anonymity. In this study, we investigate the potential for de-anonymizing users of contact tracing apps by analyzing their interactions with the system. Our results demonstrate that, in many cases, app users can be identified based on their behavior, including the number of contacts they have, the locations they visit, and the time of their interactions. Our analysis also reveals that a combination of these factors can be used to identify users with high accuracy, including 99.9% for a specific user. These findings have significant implications for the design and implementation of contact tracing apps, including the need to collect additional data to protect user anonymity.

Neural systems, comprising cells called neurons, are ubiquitous in nature and man-made entities, underlying the functioning of living organisms, including those of plants and animals, as well as robots. These neurons, however, are not the only information carriers in these systems, as quantum effects may also be present, with implications for information processing in the brain. This work delves into the potential quantum properties of neurons, including coherence, entanglement, and interactions with the environment, and explores the limitations of current knowledge in this area. It also examines the broader context of quantum effects in the brain, including microtubules, and discusses the relevance of quantum information in understanding neural systems, including their functioning in the brain, as well as the potential for quantum effects to play a role in the emergence of consciousness.

This research paper introduces a tool for automatically translating ACL2 representations of C code into executable C code and verifying its correctness through the creation of accompanying ACL2 theorems.

A cluster of young asteroids, Iochroma, has a distinctive group of over 20 members.  39991 Iochroma itself is one of these, discovered in 1998.  By analyzing Iochroma's family, we found that 18 members are within the 3:2 mean motion resonance with Jupiter, and the formation of Iochroma's members within this resonance is statistically significant.  Furthermore, our model of Iochroma's evolution shows that the family is still young, with the effects of resonant chaos not yet causing significant orbital changes.  This implies that Iochroma's members were captured into the resonance after their formation, and we suggest that this occurred due to the 2:1 mean motion resonance with Pluto, which is nearby in orbital space.

Building on the work of Ramanujan and later expanded by Adhikari, Chowla, and Kronecker, specific cases of the Riemann zeta function at odd integer values have significant historical context. A novel identity for odd integer values of the zeta function is derived in this study, and its proof relies on properties of the Hurwitz zeta function. Several corollaries of this identity are presented, which recover existing identities found by Ramanujan and other mathematicians.

We calculate the rational circle-equivariant cohomology with help of elliptic cohomology for complex projective spaces formed from any vector space, and establish that the resulting cohomology theory is an elliptic formal group scheme defined over the rational numbers.

We've developed novel machine learning models that incorporate symbolic dynamics to tackle complex physics problems rooted in algebraic geometry. Our approach addresses challenges in finding exact solutions to non-linear PDEs and their associated algebraic structures. By leveraging the connection between physics and mathematics, we've established a framework for translating physical problems into algebraic forms, which we've used to create symbolic dynamics-based machine learning models. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in uncovering hidden algebraic structures within non-linear PDEs and their solutions.

We have conducted an in-depth analysis of the $J/\psi$ angular distributions in $e^{+}e^{-}$ collisions at the LHCb's energy of 10.6 GeV, specifically for $J/\psi + \eta_c$ and $J/\psi + \chi_{cJ}$ reactions. Our research focused on $\mathcal{B}(e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi + \eta_c)$ and the $J/L$ asymmetry, which is defined as the difference in production rates between $J/\psi$ and $J/\psi + \chi_{cJ}$. Our calculations were based on a next-to-leading-order (NLO) QCD approximation within the non-relativistic QCD (NRQCD) framework. Our findings indicate that our predictions for $\mathcal{B}(e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi + \eta_c)$ and the $J/L$ asymmetry are in good agreement with the data from the LHCb. Our research also suggests that our NLO calculations provide a more accurate representation of the data than previous calculations. Our study further reveals that $\mathcal{B}(e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi + \eta_c)$ is relatively insensitive to variations in the $\alpha_s$ and $\mu$ values, which provides a more reliable estimate. Our findings also indicate that our predictions for $\mathcal{B

Our research explores the perspectives of eager and relaxed signal users regarding the purpose and significance of the Signal app's PIN feature. Through an online survey, we gathered insights from 200 Signal users, who were asked about their thoughts on the significance of PINs, their own usage, and the characteristics of their chosen PINs. The results show that most users are not aware of the security benefits provided by PINs, with a significant number believing they serve no practical purpose. While some users have created PINs, a significant number have not, and those who have do not perceive them as highly secure. The study's findings suggest a need for improved user education on the security features of Signal and the importance of setting up a PIN for enhanced security.

A novel technique has been developed to efficiently process solar energy data, enhancing traditional methods like the trapezoidal rule and quadrature. This new approach, known as solar-weighted Gaussian quadrature, is an adaptive integration method that utilizes solar irradiance data, which is then used to solve differential equations. By using this method, a simulation of the sun's behavior in a phase-space model was conducted, resulting in significant improvements in accuracy and speed. Compared to other methods, the new quadrature achieved a 20% decrease in computational time and increased accuracy by at least one order of magnitude, particularly in modeling solar energy data. This method has the potential to be applied to various scientific fields, including astrophysics, chemistry, and biology, where non-exponential decay phenomena are observed.

The curvature information of the Hessian matrix is crucial for training deep neural networks, but approximating the exact Hessian matrix often leads to an increase in computational complexity. A promising alternative is to approximate the generalized Gauss-Newton matrix at a lower rank, but this approximation can significantly affect the accuracy of the model. Our research introduces a novel approximation method for the generalized Gauss-Newton matrix, which outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods. This approximation method is based on the singular value decomposition of the matrix, and it allows for a more accurate representation of the matrix's curvature information. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approximation method through experiments on image classification and image regression tasks, and we show that it leads to a significant improvement in the convergence rate of the model.

German multilingual models trained on various gender systems demonstrate that the most recent systems implemented in Germany have a profound impact on the gender associations of nouns within the models.

We investigate the properties of stiffness and charmability in a broad category of 
groups that includes many important examples such as $Sp_n(\mathcal O_S)$ and $Spin_{2n+1}(\mathcal O_S)$. 
Our approach involves a key finding that a finite-index subgroup of a stiff 
discrete group retains its stiffness. 
This leads to a useful criterion for determining if such groups are charming based on 
their finite quotients. 
Additionally, this criterion has a direct application in resolving the 
Kneser-Tits conjecture for $Spin_{2n+1}(\mathcal O_S)$ when the set of primes $\mathcal O_S$ contains at most one odd prime.

This paper introduces a novel zero-shot category-level object pose estimation task. 
In this setup, object pose generalization occurs across categories during deployment, 
as opposed to training. A key challenge lies in handling within-class variations 
and object occlusions due to the unknown test categories. To address this issue, 
we propose a data-driven method that utilizes object point clouds and multimodal 
semantic category-level object detection results. 
Our approach involves learning a robust object pose prior from a large-scale 
dataset and a category-specific point-to-surface alignment module. 
A comprehensive benchmark based on the CUB dataset is used to evaluate the 
proposed method's performance, and our experiments demonstrate the method's 
ability to accurately estimate object poses for categories it was not trained on.

Predicting traffic on a massive scale is a complex task due to the vast number of possible outcomes.
The effectiveness of current forecasting techniques is often hindered by the large number of inputs,
resulting in overfitting and inaccurate predictions.
In this paper, a new approach is proposed to tackle this issue by reducing the number of features
on a large road network using similarity-based analysis.
By grouping roads with similar traffic patterns, a smaller set of representative features can be extracted,
which can then be used to forecast traffic on an unseen dataset.
Through extensive experiments on a large real-world dataset, the proposed method demonstrates significant
improvements in forecasting accuracy and efficiency, outperforming state-of-the-art methods.

Current methods for simulating hypothetical scenarios in complex systems rely heavily on labor-intensive, costly, and error-prone manual processes.  To address this issue, novel algorithms have been developed to automatically generate these simulations.  This research focuses on enhancing the capacity of Variational Graph Autoencoders to accurately model and predict the effects of altering a system's causal structure.  To accomplish this, a unique variant of VGE called VACA is proposed, which is specifically designed to capture the underlying dynamics of graphical models.  To evaluate the effectiveness of VACA, both controlled experiments and real-world applications are conducted.  This variant of VGE is shown to outperform existing approaches in a variety of critical tasks, including predicting outcomes under untested conditions and identifying which factors are most influential in determining that outcome.

Developing an efficient system to detect transient sky phenomena in real-time is crucial for the success of pulsar and fast transient research. Pulsar research requires precise real-time identification of periodic signals, while fast transient research demands the detection of millisecond-duration signals. To achieve this, low-cost, real-time capable systems are necessary. The REAL-time Transmission Acquisition (REALTA) system, designed for real-time signal processing, is capable of identifying transients in real-time with a latency of 100 milliseconds. This system was integrated into the Irish LOFAR station in 2019, enabling real-time detection of fast radio bursts (FRBs) and periodic signals. In this paper, we outline the design and functionality of REALTA, and present initial findings from its operation at Markhill, including the discovery of periodic signals and FRBs.

The incorporation of machine learning and artificial intelligence in metaphotonics is revolutionizing the design of advanced photonic systems. This integration is enabling the development of complex, multi-functional photonic devices that were previously unattainable through conventional methods. This review explores the progress in AI-driven metaphotonics, encompassing recent advancements in ML and AI techniques, their applications in photonics, and the challenges ahead. By harnessing AI and ML, researchers can now optimize the performance of existing photonic devices and discover novel solutions to longstanding problems in the field.

This study examines a comprehensive dataset of 1.1 million movies, spanning from 1890 to 2020, and delves into the influence of pre-released attributes on box office revenue. By analyzing a substantial dataset, we identify a significant correlation between pre-release metadata and movie earnings. Specifically, we found that certain attributes, such as the presence of prominent actors, directors, or specific genres, can predict box office success with a notable degree of accuracy. Furthermore, we discovered that the accuracy of our predictions increases as the number of attributes available for analysis increases. Our research also reveals that the accuracy of our predictions is relatively consistent across different time periods, with a notable exception for the recent years of 2018-2020, which may be attributed to the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on movie earnings.

We examine the interaction between secondary frequency control and voltage dynamics in interconnected power grids, taking into account the stabilization effects of both phenomena. The analysis is based on a detailed mathematical model that accurately represents frequency control, voltage dynamics, and the interconnected nature of power grids. The research reveals that secondary frequency control can significantly impact voltage dynamics, even though the typically considered effects are found to be negligible. The model's accuracy is validated through the analysis of actual data from the Swedish power grid.

Cyber Physical Systems (CPS) are engineered to integrate and control physical processes through cyber systems, enabling applications such as smart manufacturing, autonomous vehicles, and power grids. As these technologies evolve, there is a growing need for complex systems of systems that can adapt to unpredictable environments. To meet this demand, we propose the concept of Intelligent Cyber Physical Systems of Systems (I-CPS2), which incorporates advanced AI capabilities to enhance decision-making and operational efficiency. This framework is exemplified by the deployment of I-CPS2 in smart manufacturing environments, where it is used to optimize production lines and resource allocation. By leveraging I-CPS2, manufacturers can achieve greater flexibility and resilience in the face of changing market conditions and unexpected disruptions.

Blazars with specific types of line emission spectra show an unusual increase in ultraviolet and soft X-ray wavelengths. This unique pattern is difficult to explain using standard models of how light is generated and scattered. In this study, we investigate the possibility that this excess light is caused by high-energy electrons in the jet scattering ambient light through a process called external Compton scattering. We found that the standard model of light scattering cannot explain the observed UV excess, but a more complex model that takes into account the polarization of the scattered light can explain the observed patterns. This suggests that the observed patterns may be the result of a complex interplay between different physical processes in the jet.

In the context of string theory, a significant challenge arises from the intricate arrangement of vacua, characterized by their vast number and complex structure.  This complexity hinders conventional numerical methods, which are often applied to simpler systems.  To address this limitation, researchers have developed an innovative approach, utilizing an adaptive path-finding algorithm that enables the traversal of the theory's complex structure, across the barriers that impede standard methods.  By employing this technique, researchers have successfully extended their analysis to more complex theories, such as type IIB string theory with both flux and D-brane sources, where it has been observed that the number of vacua is significantly larger than previously estimated, with notable implications for the cosmological constant and the multiverse hypothesis.

We develop and analyze two strategies for identifying the best possible measurement to distinguish between two pure states when using an online approach. The first, called "Hindsight," relies on prior knowledge of the distribution of the states, while "Regret Minimization" adapts to the states without any initial information. The effectiveness of these algorithms is measured by their regret, which quantifies the number of mistakes made. The results show that, in a scenario where the states' overlap is small, "Hindsight" can make at most $O(\sqrt{T\log(1/\delta)})$ mistakes over $T$ trials, given the probability of failure is at most $\delta$. Meanwhile, "Regret Minimization" makes at most $O(\sqrt{T}\arccos(\sqrt{1-\delta^2}/2))$ mistakes without knowing the states' overlap. Furthermore, "Regret Minization" is shown to be optimal in terms of minimizing regret in this specific setting.

Baryon creation is investigated using a quantized fragmentation model based on QCD strings. Baryons are envisioned as QCD strings with twisted structures. The energy required to separate string endpoints is calculated using a energy per unit length function. String fragmentation occurs when it exceeds this energy. The resulting baryon mass distribution follows a Fermi-Dirac statistical pattern. The model's predictions for string twist and tension are compared with data from the BESIII experiment on $\psi(3770) \to K^+K^- \Lambda_c^+ \bar{\Lambda_c}^-$, and the findings support a specific type of string twist known as the $k=1$ mode.

The travel-time measurements for north-south sound waves around active regions in the sun show significant differences compared to those in the east-west direction. To understand this discrepancy, researchers analyzed data from simulations of the solar interior and found that the dominant factor contributing to the travel-time measurements is the flow along with the rotation of the sun. The results indicate that when considering only the flow and rotation, the travel-time measurements in the east-west direction are similar to those in the north-south direction. The difference in travel times is mainly due to the way the flow and rotation are oriented in space. The simulations suggest that the observed travel-time differences are a natural consequence of the flow and rotation in the solar interior.

Using numerical simulations, we investigate the impact of primordial magnetic fields on the formation of galactic halos and the generation of gravitational waves. Our analysis reveals that the gravitational waves produced by magnetohydrodynamic turbulence in galactic halos exhibit a characteristic stochastic background with a non-standard frequency dependence. Specifically, we find that this background peaks at frequencies around 1 Hertz and decreases with a rate of five-halves below that point. This behavior contrasts with standard cosmological models, which predict a zero-slope frequency dependence at lower frequencies. Furthermore, our results suggest that the gravitational waves produced by such models could be detected by arrays of pulsar timing arrays, offering a means to probe the properties of primordial magnetic fields and their role in galaxy formation.

Light field data is typically stored in a 4-dimensional format, comprising multiple images representing various viewing angles. This redundancy can be leveraged by compressing the data using techniques that exploit the different views' relationships. However, conventional compression methods often neglect the spatial connections between these views, resulting in subpar compression ratios. In this research, a novel, data-driven approach is presented to compress the light field data using its various images' correlations. This method employs a unique, lightweight neural network that processes the data's disparity map to extract essential information from each view, enabling efficient compression. The proposed technique achieves impressive compression ratios of up to 10.66 times, surpassing existing methods by a significant margin.

Current neural vector-based cross-lingual information retrieval systems primarily rely on either interactive or non-interactive models, each with its limitations. By combining the strengths of both approaches, we propose a novel hybrid model that effectively addresses these drawbacks. Furthermore, we introduce a data augmentation technique, further enhancing the performance of our system. Our experiments demonstrate the superiority of our approach over existing state-of-the-art systems.

This study compares two statistical methods for generating small-area estimates of HIV prevalence in African nations, specifically design-based and model-based techniques. We utilized national survey data from the Demographic and Health Surveys for 28 African countries, including 8 from low and middle-income nations, to assess the accuracy of these methods. The design-based approach involved analyzing each region's data separately using complex sampling methods, while the model-based approach employed multilevel Bayesian inference to integrate region, neighborhood, and country-level data. We found that the design-based approach often produced unreliable estimates due to insufficient data in some regions, resulting in large standard errors and bias. In contrast, the model-based approach provided more accurate and precise estimates by leveraging both regional and country-level information. Furthermore, the model-based approach outperformed the design-based approach in terms of bias and standard error. Our results suggest that the model-based approach is a more effective tool for generating small-area estimates in low and middle-income nations, particularly when regional data is limited.

The study of two-dimensional materials' properties, particularly their electronic and optical characteristics, is crucial for the development of future nanoscale devices. By investigating the maletene compounds of the form MA$_2$Z$_4$, researchers have found that the electronic band structure and optical properties of these materials can be influenced by the way the layers are stacked. However, the study has also identified the existence of a specific type of exciton that is not dependent on the stacking configuration. By analyzing the quasiparticle band alignment and the optical properties of these materials, researchers have identified the key factors that influence their electronic and optical characteristics. The study has also identified the experimental techniques required to verify the findings and has provided insights into the potential applications of these materials in nanoscale devices.

The search for $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decays utilizing $pp$ collision data collected by LHCb, with a combined total of 9 million muon pairs at center-of-gravity energies of 7 and 8 TeV in 2011 and 2012, yields 4 standard deviations of significant evidence for these decays. Analysis of the mass distribution of the $p \mu^+ \mu^-$ final state provides constraints on the differential branching fraction.

A detailed analysis of a computer model of a star-forming process reveals that the formation of a disk in a star system is a natural outcome of the collapse of a star's surrounding material. The model shows that a disk forms when the material's angular momentum prevents it from collapsing into a star. The model also indicates that a disk forms in a star system when the material's angular momentum is high enough to overcome the effects of gravity. The model also suggests that a disk forms in a star system when the material's angular momentum is not significantly affected by the material's gravity. Astronomical observations through the Very Large Telescope's ESO Very Large Telescope SpectroPolarimetric Image Cutout System are often compromised by the dispersion of Earth's atmosphere, necessitating the use of dispersion compensators. To optimize these compensators, researchers rely on accurate on-sky measurements of atmospheric dispersion, which are typically modeled using a single or multiple wavelength-dependent curves. This study presents an in-depth analysis of the reliability of two atmospheric dispersion models by examining VLT/VLTCS data across the 350-950 nm wavelength range under diverse atmospheric conditions. The findings indicate that both models agree within their error margins, which are consistent with previous VLT/VLTCS measurements of the atmosphere. Notably, both models agree with theoretical predictions of the atmosphere's group index, which are also consistent with previous VLT/VLTCS measurements of the atmosphere. The variability in the atmosphere's dispersion is attributed to fluctuations in the atmosphere's water vapor content, which can be mitigated by using observations taken in narrow spectral bands.

This study introduces a novel Bayesian method for the robust modeling of multiple time series, which simultaneously captures the individual characteristics of each series and their shared underlying patterns. Our approach employs a hierarchical Bayesian model that integrates the sparse and differentiable properties of Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) to effectively reduce the dimensionality of the time series data. By leveraging the sparse property, we can uncover the intrinsic common factors driving the time series and identify the key underlying drivers. By leveraging the differentiable property, we can capture the unique components and differences within each time series. Our method is highly efficient and scalable, capable of processing large datasets. Our approach is evaluated on both simulated and real-world datasets, where we compare its performance against state-of-the-art methods for multi-period time series modeling. Our results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms the competing approaches in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

This brief note establishes a connection between Pontryagin duality and continuous logic, specifically for locally compact Abelian groups, by defining a continuous logic language tailored to such groups and demonstrating a correspondence between their duals, an elementary equivalence relationship, and a Tarsin-Vaught test for certain types of group mappings.

This work explores the application of Federated Learning (FL) in creating equitable and secure machine learning models. It delves into the characteristics of Federated Learning that are crucial for developing fair models and secure frameworks. The study also compares the security and fairness of centralized and distributed machine learning approaches. Furthermore, it provides a framework for integrating differential privacy and adversarial training into Federated Learning to develop secure and fair models. The work concludes by offering a roadmap for future research in this area.

In the supersymmetric minimal $U(1)_X$ model, where $U(1)_X$ is a hidden sector gauge group, the dark matter is composed of a right-handed neutrino, $N_1$, which is a singlet under the Standard Model gauge group. The model's $U(1)_X$ symmetry is broken at the $10^{12}$ GeV scale, which is necessary for the correct relic density of $N_1$. The breaking of $U(1)_X$ is facilitated by a superpotential term, $\lambda_S S \Phi_1 \Phi_1$, where $S$ is a chiral superfield whose scalar component acquires a vacuum expectation value. The model's parameters are constrained by electroweak and dark matter observables, with the $Z N_1 N_1$ interaction playing a crucial role in the dark matter relic density. The model is analyzed using a combination of renormalization group evolution and numerical calculations, with the result being consistent with the observed relic density of $N_1$.

In a wireless-powered network where devices receive energy and transmit data through an intelligent meta-surface, we investigate a throughput maximization issue. The device with the strongest power connection to the base station is chosen to transmit data, but this decision leads to suboptimal throughput. The interplay between data transmission and wireless power transfer, combined with signal reflection and hardware limitations, complicates the problem, rendering it non-convex. The problem is further complicated by the presence of interference from the base station to the receiver. The problem is solved using a deep learning method, specifically a two-stage unsupervised learning approach, where the first stage involves optimizing power allocation and the second stage involves optimizing phase shifts. The proposed approach is shown to be efficient and yields significant performance improvements compared to benchmark schemes.

The study of the decay of $^{186}$Hg, a neutron-rich isotope, has been
investigated through $\gamma$-ray spectroscopy following its creation via the
$^{198}$Pt($^{20}$Ne, $^{17}$F) reaction. This is the first time the decay of
$^{186}$Hg has been studied in detail. A wide range of transitions, spanning
the entire energy spectrum of $^{186}$Hg, have been identified and their
properties have been analyzed. A significant finding is that $^{186}$Hg's decay
pattern is similar to that of $^{184}$Hg, suggesting a shared quadrupole
deformed ground state. Additionally, a new isomeric state at 103 keV with a
half-life of 1.2(2) ms has been discovered. This research provides a more
comprehensive understanding of the decay properties of $^{186}$Hg, which is
essential for a deeper comprehension of nuclear structure in this area.

We explore the intersection of dark matter and leptogenesis within a unified framework. Our approach involves a scalar field that breaks lepton number symmetry and a fermion, which is a candidate for dark matter and interacts with the scalar field through a cubic interaction. The scalar field's presence during the dark matter annihilation process amplifies it, resulting in a suitable dark matter abundance. Furthermore, the enhanced scalar field also generates a significant lepton asymmetry, which can be subsequently converted into a baryon asymmetry through sphaleron processes. Our findings indicate that the lepton asymmetry produced can be sufficient to account for the observed baryon asymmetry in the universe.

This study introduces a novel control approach, known as the Successive Side Information-diffused Actor-Critic (SSII-AC), which is capable of mastering multiple tasks sequentially while leveraging information from each preceding task. The proposed algorithm, SSII-AC, is designed to tackle complex control challenges, such as navigation and manipulation, where the state space is continuous and the action space involves both discrete and continuous components. The algorithm's success in learning diverse tasks, such as movement and object manipulation, is demonstrated using a limited dataset, obtained from the extensive exploration of a single agent, which is then reused across multiple tasks. The proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art control algorithms, such as the Actor-Critic (AC) and Multi-task Actor-Critic (MT-AC), when the state space is large and the number of tasks is significant.

We examine the complex plane representation of the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory, involving three two-dimensional scalar fields linked to the Casimir operators of $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ at level $k$. By deriving two non-trivial Ward identities applicable to three- and four-point correlations of the theory's identity operator, we obtain two distinct sets of equations governing the dependence of four-point correlations on complex plane coordinates. Notably, one set of equations corresponds to the standard conformal field theory stress tensor conservation law. We resolve these equations to derive two separate sets of four-point correlation functions, ultimately comparing them with conformal block calculations to validate our findings.

Despite GANs' success in generating realistic images, produced GANs often fall short in the quality of their content, particularly in relation to specific attributes within those images. To address this limitation, researchers have developed ABLABNs, which incorporate binary labels into the loss function. However, this approach is limited as it cannot effectively handle continuous values or complex relationships. To overcome these limitations, we introduce the Relation GAN, which utilizes a more versatile loss function that can handle continuous values and relationships. This loss function, known as triplet margin loss, enables the GAN to learn relationships between attributes within an image. As a result, our GAN achieves superior performance in generating realistic images, particularly when it comes to the accuracy of the relationships within those images.

A novel approach to enhancing the range of quantum key distribution networks is the typical Bell-state measurement employed in the twin-field protocol, which is susceptible to a potential eavesdropper's attack. This study introduces a variation of the TF protocol, which is resistant to the specific type of attack, and is implementable without the need for precise phase synchronization between Alice and Bob. The protocol's range is comparable to that of phase-synchronized TF QKD, and it is also capable of withstanding the phase-flip attack, thereby increasing its distance from Alice and Bob to approximately 100 km.

For each unitary operator $U$ on a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$, the C*-algebra generated by the Toeplitz operator $T(\zeta)$ and $U$ on Bessel-type reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions is studied. A specific type of space is considered, where point evaluations by elements of the unit ball in $\mathbb{C}^n$ are defined. The space in question is the Segal-Bargmann-Fock space, and its corresponding Toeplitz C*-algebra is denoted as $\mathcal{T}_*^n$. The structure of this algebra is investigated, and it is found that $\mathcal{T}_*^n$ is a simple, nuclear, and separative algebra that satisfies the Universal Property. The relationship between $\mathcal{T}_*^n$ and K-theory is also explored, and it is found that the boundary map in the six-term exact sequence is surjective, which is a direct consequence of a surjective algebraic boundary map.

Detecting uncommon and rare items in vast arrays of data is a significant challenge in the field of computer vision. Conventional object detection methods are hindered by the labor-intensive process of creating precise bounding box annotations for each item, which is particularly time-consuming and costly for vast datasets. To address this issue, we've developed an innovative approach to large-scale object detection that utilizes prior knowledge from pre-existing datasets to automatically generate training data for the task. Our method involves creating a large dataset of images with minimal modifications, which can then be used to train a model to recognize these items. Our approach has been shown to outperform current state-of-the-art methods on multiple benchmarks, including the COCO-OD1M and Flamingo datasets, and has been made available for public use.

The S1 ionization complex, a prominent HII region in the Rho Ophiuchus molecular cloud, is primarily powered by the T Tauri star S1. To understand the interplay between these components, we conducted a multi-wavelength study using ALMA, Herschel, Spitzer, and Chandra data. Our analysis revealed that the ionized gas surrounding S1 is spatially connected to the PDR and molecular gas regions, indicating a close relationship between these different gas phases. Observations of [CII] emission and ionized gas show a significant gas flow from the PDR to the ionized region, suggesting that the ionization of the gas is not uniform. Additionally, our study found that the PDR is located on the far side of the molecular gas, indicating that the ionization of the gas is not uniform. Our study also revealed that the PDR is located on the far side of the molecular gas, indicating that the ionization of the gas is not uniform.

The remarkable success of Transformer models in natural language processing tasks has piqued the interest of computer vision researchers, prompting a concerted effort to apply and adapt these models to visual tasks. A primary advantage of Transformer models lies in their inherent ability to capture long-range relationships and their scalability without the increasing complexity often associated with depth. This survey aims to provide a concise overview of the fundamental concepts behind Transformer models and their core variants, as well as their applications in vision tasks. We will also explore the benefits and constraints of employing Transformer models in vision, and identify promising avenues for future investigation.

Mortality forecasting models based on the Lee-Carter approach have shown to be effective in predicting future mortality rates. A factor model can also be used to make similar predictions, and a decision needs to be made on whether the factor model's factor loadings should remain constant or change over time. This study compares the performance of the Lee-Carter model with two factor models - one with time-invariant factor loadings and another with time-varying factor loadings - to determine which is the most suitable for forecasting. The analysis uses real-world data from the US and Italy, and a decision tree method is employed to select the best model for each area. The results indicate that the time-invariant factor model outperforms both the Lee-Carter model and the time-varying factor model in the US, and that the time-varying factor model is superior to the Lee-Carter model in Italy.

Research into Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has yielded impressive results, yet its search process is susceptible to interference from unrelated, low-quality designs. We investigate the impact of interference on NAS and develop methods to mitigate it, focusing on two prominent algorithms: DARTS and ENAS. Our analysis reveals that a straightforward approach of eliminating interference significantly accelerates search convergence. Moreover, a dynamic strategy that minimizes interference during search yields even better outcomes. We validate the efficacy of these techniques across various settings and datasets, including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, CIFAR-100-N, and Tiny-ImageNet.

Time series analysis is a crucial aspect of statistical analysis, and its significance is amplified by the substantial increase in available data. The evolution of time series analysis has been marked by the introduction of essential techniques such as exponential smoothing, autoregressive models, and moving averages, all of which have been further enhanced by the development of open-source software like the theft package for R. This package provides a comprehensive suite of tools for time series analysis, including feature extraction, similarity-based analysis, and time series decomposition, among others. This article delves into the capabilities of the theft package and showcases its core functionalities through practical examples.
We identify concrete, infinitely precise criteria under which a proper geodesically complete CAT(0) space has a semistable fundamental at its boundary.

Human-assisted translation is a common practice in the translation industry, but its effectiveness is often hindered by the difficulty in gauging human-assisted translators' reliability. To address this issue, we propose a Bayesian method for evaluating human-assisted translations. This approach leverages both the translated and original texts to assess translator performance. We compare our novel assessment model against conventional metrics used to evaluate human-assisted translations.

In general scattering scenarios, there's a specific set of initial states known as eigenchannels, which have a specific affinity towards certain directions of the system, resulting in minimal interaction with the system. This paper derives mathematical constraints, called sum rules, that limit the possibility of such non-interacting states existing, based on the characteristics of the scattering setup and the properties of the system's potential. These rules are formulated in a mathematical framework that takes into consideration the complexities of the scattering setup and the properties of the system's potential. To validate these mathematical constraints, this paper demonstrates their application in a specific real-world scattering scenario, which involves the scattering of electrons with a specific molecular structure.

Deep neural networks are often criticized for their high computational requirements and substantial memory usage. To address these issues, researchers have developed feature selection methods to eliminate unnecessary connections. This study focuses on determining if the convolutional neural network architecture is indeed the superior choice over fully connected networks in terms of pruning efficiency. Our experiments, which involved pruning both types of networks to achieve a 99.5% reduction in weights, revealed that the NNCCS method reduced weights by 99.8% on CIFAR10 and 99.9% on CIFAR100 datasets while maintaining accuracy above 90% for both datasets. These fully connected networks performed comparably to their fully trained counterparts, whereas the baseline method achieved 93.1% accuracy on CIFAR10 and 90.6% accuracy on CIFAR100. Additionally, we found that the NNCS method reduced weights by 99.9% on both datasets while maintaining accuracy above 90% for both datasets, and it outperformed the baseline method by reducing weights by 1.1% on the CIFAR100 dataset. Our results indicate that NNCS method is more effective than the baseline method, and NNCS method achieved a 99.9% reduction in weights while maintaining accuracy above 90% for both datasets.

We examine a scenario where a seller offers a large number of tickets in a multi-stage game of chance. The game reveals winning tickets over time, and at each stage, buyers can choose to purchase tickets from the seller or hold onto a previously bought ticket that hasn't yet revealed its outcome. The game ends when all tickets have been checked, and the total earnings are divided by the number of tickets initially sold. The central question we investigate is how the seller can set prices to maximize their total revenue, and what the optimal buying strategy is for the buyers, in a game that unfolds in several stages.

The large-charge expansion technique has yielded precise predictions for the spectrum of $O(N)$-symmetric theories at zero temperature, specifically for the anomalous dimensions of multi-charge operators $\phi^Q$ as functions of the coupling in the critical regime. We have computed the anomalous dimensions to a higher order (equivalent to six-loop precision) using this approach, which is valid beyond the initial leading order approximation. This advancement complements recent findings from the conformal field theory of higher-spin operators and the large-$Q$ limit of the BPS sector in four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=4$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory.

Our research reveals that certain electron-phonon interactions, which were previously thought to be negligible, can significantly influence the dynamics of valley physics in two-dimensional materials. Specifically, we discovered that the Coulomb interaction mediated by phonons, which is a long-range mechanism, can substantially affect valley Hall responses, contrasting with the short-range deformation potential coupling that we also investigated. This novel insight has far-reaching implications for understanding valley physics in two-dimensional materials, as it necessitates a reevaluation of existing theories and predictions.

The VisDA 2022 Challenge seeks unsupervised domain adaptation solutions for visual tasks, where models trained on source domains (synthetically generated) need to perform well on target domains (real-world images) without direct access to target domain labels. The goal is to adapt models trained on the WSCoD source domain to achieve the best unsupervised results on WSCoD2022, with a notable emphasis on unimodal settings. Our top-scoring solution, a combination of multiple adaptation techniques, integrates the following: 1) an approach that aligns source and target domains using both image and feature distributions, incorporating image-level and feature distribution knowledge transfer, as well as adversarial learning; 2) a method that leverages self-supervised learning to enhance domain invariance and feature quality, using a combination of multiple self-supervised tasks; 3) an approach that utilizes semantic information to guide domain adaptation, incorporating cross-modal retrieval and semantic alignment. The integration of these techniques results in significant performance gains, achieving a 20.1% improvement in mean average precision (mAP) and a 20.6% improvement in recall rate compared to a baseline.

t-SNE is a widely used technique for visualizing high-dimensional data in lower dimensions, but it relies on Euclidean distance, which may not be suitable for data that lies on a sphere. This paper introduces VMF-SNE, an extension of t-SNE that incorporates the properties of the spherical von Mises-Fisher distribution to create more effective embeddings for spherical data. By leveraging the unique characteristics of the sphere, VMF-SNE can generate better data representations, outperforming both traditional t-SNE and other manifold learning methods, such as UMAP and spectral methods, in various benchmark tests.

The study also shows that the convergence rate of the method is influenced by the filling fraction of the surrounding environment.
A key discovery is that the convergence of the method occurs at the same point for the polaron's energy and the self-energy.
This implies that the method's efficacy in the weakly bound dimer regime is not solely determined by the binding energy.
